item.title: The liberation of East Bengal, continuum. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In 1947, August 14 was observed as a “Day of Liberation” by many Muslims of British India, particularly Bengali Muslims. It marked the culmination of successive revolts, political movements, and popular protests against nearly 190 years of British colonial rule.
History, however, is rarely allowed to remain whole. Bengali Muslims have repeatedly neglected -- or consciously erased -- the sacrifices of those who struggled in earlier chapters of their political emancipation.
The martyrs, activists and leaders of the pre-1947 movements, along with the families who bore the consequences of their sacrifices, have largely disappeared from public memory.
Even those who surrendered careers, security, and personal comfort for the creation of East Pakistan were later made to feel ashamed of their role. Whatever its subsequent failures and contradictions, East Pakistan formed the territorial and political foundation from which independent Bangladesh ultimately emerged.
A similar danger confronts our understanding of 1971 today.
Attempts to elevate the July 2024 uprising into an all-encompassing national narrative must not diminish the unique historical significance of the Liberation War or push earlier struggles into obscurity.
July 2024 deserves its rightful place in our national history -- but not at the expense of 1971, just as 1971 should not require the erasure of 1947 or the long resistance that preceded it.
Some observers describe this recurring rejection of our own historical inheritance as the symptom of an “ungrateful nation.” Whether or not one accepts that harsh judgment, the underlying question cannot be avoided: Can Bangladesh build an honest and confident future while repeatedly denying the people, movements, and sacrifices that made each successive stage of its freedom possible?
Bangladesh was not born from a single day, a single movement, or the vision of a single leader. Its emergence was the outcome of a long and unfinished struggle by ordinary people -- peasants, workers, religious reformers, students, intellectuals, soldiers and political organizers -- against exploitation, foreign domination, economic injustice, and authoritarian rule.
The decisive events of 1971 occupy a unique and inviolable place in our national history. Yet 1971 itself did not arise in a historical vacuum. It inherited ideas, grievances, organizational experience, and traditions of resistance accumulated over more than two centuries.
Likewise, the July Revolution of 2024 did not invalidate 1971. It expressed a later generation’s determination to recover democratic rights that independence had promised but successive governments had too often denied.
The proper metaphor for our history is therefore not a collection of competing monuments. It is a river. Many streams entered it at different times. Some carried religious reform, some agrarian justice, some Bengali cultural identity, some Muslim political emancipation, some provincial autonomy and others representative democracy.
They did not always flow peacefully together, and they cannot all be judged identically. Nevertheless, each contributed to the historical experience from which Bangladesh emerged.
After the Battle of Plassey in 1757, the East India Company’s power grew through revenue extraction, commercial monopoly, and the restructuring of Bengal’s rural economy. Those who resisted were not always equipped with modern political programs. They acted in the language and institutions available to them.
The Fakir-Sannyasi Resistance (1760-1800) brought Muslim fakirs and Hindu ascetics, together with sections of the rural population, into conflict with Company authority.
The Faraizi Movement(1818-1860) led by Haji Shariatullah and subsequently Dudu Miyan combined Islamic reform with the mobilization of impoverished cultivators.
Titumir (1831) challenged oppressive levies, landlords, and colonial power before making his last stand at Narkelbaria.
During the Indigo Revolt(1859-1860), cultivators collectively refused to grow a crop imposed upon them through coercive arrangements.
These struggles differed in leadership, territory, and ideology.
It would be misleading to force every one of them into the mould of twentieth-century nationalism. But it would be equally misleading to dismiss them because they lacked our present political vocabulary.
In their own circumstances, they asserted a fundamental principle: Those who cultivate the land and bear the burdens of society are entitled to justice and human dignity.
The same historical sympathy should be extended to the participants in the uprising of 1857, including those involved in resistance in Dhaka and elsewhere in eastern Bengal.
Later came the controversies surrounding the 1905 Partition of Bengal and its annulment in 1911. Hindu and Muslim communities did not always understand those developments in the same way.
Many Muslims of Eastern Bengal saw the new province, with Dhaka as its capital, as an opportunity for education, employment, and political recognition. Many anti-partition nationalists viewed the division as a colonial strategy.
Honest history must preserve both experiences rather than suppressing one to simplify the other.
The Tebhaga movement of the 1940s similarly demanded a fairer share of the harvest for “ bargadars. ” Its enduring lesson is not confined to party history. It belongs to the cultivators -- including many women -- who confronted an unequal agrarian order and insisted that those producing society’s wealth should not remain permanently dispossessed.
The meaning of 1947 remains one of the most sensitive questions in Bangladesh’s historical memory. It should be approached neither through nostalgia nor through retrospective contempt.
Millions of Bengali Muslims supported the Pakistan movement because they believed a separate homeland would rescue them from political marginalization, economic deprivation, and entrenched social inequality. Their hopes were real.
The failure of Pakistan’s ruling establishment to honour those hopes does not make the original aspirations fraudulent. Nor does it erase the work and sacrifice of the people who struggled for what they understood as freedom.
For many Bengali Muslims, August 14, 1947 was a “day of liberation”. For many others, Partition brought fear, displacement, and communal suffering. Both truths belong to history.
To acknowledge the emancipatory meaning that Pakistan possessed for large numbers of Bengali Muslims is not to defend the discrimination subsequently imposed upon East Bengal.
Nor is it to weaken the sovereignty or moral foundations of Bangladesh. On the contrary, it helps explain why the people of East Pakistan reacted so powerfully when the promises of 1947 were broken.
Pakistan’s rulers denied the Bengali majority equal recognition, transferred resources disproportionately, concentrated political and military power in West Pakistan, and repeatedly obstructed representative government.
The people who had sought dignity through Pakistan gradually discovered that they were being treated as subjects within the state they had helped create.
The Liberation War was therefore both a rupture and a culmination. Bangladesh repudiated the oppressive structure of Pakistan, but it inherited the unfulfilled aspirations for dignity, equality, and representative government that had influenced Bengali Muslims before 1947.
Historical continuity does not mean that 1947 and 1971 were identical. It means that peoples often move toward freedom through successive stages, discovering through experience that one settlement has not answered all their demands.
Political independence did not automatically establish accountable institutions. During the five decades after 1971, Bangladesh achieved important advances in education, public health, women’s participation, agriculture, industry and disaster management. It also experienced assassinations, military interventions, disputed elections, corruption, partisan capture of institutions and recurring restrictions on political freedoms.
No major political party can credibly narrate this period as a story of its own innocence. Democratic institutions became vulnerable whenever leaders treated the state as party property, opponents as enemies and electoral victory as a permanent licence to rule.
Against that background, the student-led movement of July 2024 became a much wider popular uprising. What began around the quota issue expanded into resistance against repression, unaccountable government, and the closing of democratic space.
Sheikh Hasina was forced to leave office on August 5, 2024 after weeks of protest and a severe state crackdown. The uprising was followed by an interim period and, in February 2026, Bangladesh held its first parliamentary election since the fall of her government.
July should not be used to erase 1971, just as 1971 should never have been used to erase 1947, 1952, 1969, or the earlier peasant resistances. A new political order cannot establish its legitimacy by declaring that everything before it was darkness. That habit merely replaces one official mythology with another.
The participants in July did not struggle to exchange one personality cult for a new one. Their sacrifices impose a duty to establish institutions through which citizens can peacefully remove governments, criticize leaders and obtain justice without requiring another uprising.
Other countries demonstrate that national memory can accommodate successive liberations.
The United States honours its declaration of independence in 1776, while recognizing that its promise of equality remained gravely incomplete under slavery.
The abolition of slavery, reconstruction, and the civil-rights movement did not cancel the American Revolution; they compelled later generations to enlarge its meaning.
South Africa remembers resistance extending from early African opposition to dispossession through the African National Congress, the Defiance Campaign, the Soweto uprising, and the democratic transition of 1994. Nelson Mandela’s stature does not require the disappearance of all who struggled before or beside him.
Poland commemorates nineteenth-century uprisings, the restoration of independence in 1918, resistance during the Second World War, and the Solidarity movement against communist rule. Its later victories did not render its earlier, unsuccessful uprisings meaningless. Defeat itself sometimes preserved a people’s political imagination.
The lesson is clear: A mature nation does not need to choose only one generation of heroes. It can honour different stages of struggle while openly examining their limitations.
Bangladesh now requires a national philosophy of remembrance and democratic renewal founded on several principles.
First, history must be plural and evidence-based. No government or party should possess a monopoly over textbooks, archives, museums or national commemorations. Historians must be free to question cherished narratives without fear.
Second, remembrance must include ordinary people. The cultivator who refused indigo, the sharecropper who demanded “tebhaga”, the language activist, the freedom fighter, the garment worker, and the student protester all belong to the national story.
Third, recognition is not absolution. We can acknowledge a movement’s historical contribution while criticizing communalism, exclusion, political violence, or errors committed by some of its leaders.
Fourth, 1947, 1971, and 2024 should be understood in their own contexts. Each answered a different crisis. None should be weaponized to humiliate citizens whose family memories or political interpretations differ.
Fifth, the dignity of every community must be protected. Bengal’s history contains Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Christian, Indigenous, secular, and religious traditions. A national narrative that makes any community feel like a temporary guest betrays the experience of Bengal itself.
Sixth, the rule of law must replace the cycle of revenge. Accountability should rest on evidence, independent courts and due process -- not collective punishment or partisan justice.
Finally, the aspirations of every movement must be translated into durable institutions: Honest elections, an independent judiciary, a professional administration, accountable security forces, a free press, local government, and enforceable protections for citizens and political minorities.
Democracy means more than defeating an unpopular ruler. It means ensuring that no future ruler can accumulate the same unchecked power.
The greatest tribute to past sacrifices is not another statue or slogan. It is a Republic in which people no longer need to sacrifice their lives merely to secure the right to speak, vote, and live with dignity.
Bangladesh’s history is not a contest in which one liberation survives only by destroying the memory of another.
It is a cumulative inheritance. From the cultivators who resisted Company oppression to those who demanded Muslim political emancipation; from the martyrs of the Language Movement to the freedom fighters of 1971; and from generations who defended democracy to the young people of July 2024 -- each carried forward an unfinished demand for justice.
A nation confident in its identity can remember them all.
Mohiuddin Zaman is a retired Canadian Banker of Bangladesh origin.

item.title: Why the ivory tower must fall. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Science was never meant to be set in stone. It is a relentless, self-correcting quest for truth driven by trial and error. Yet, we are living through a baffling paradox: At the exact moment human genius is rewriting genomes and birthing artificial intelligence, public trust in the scientific community is hitting rock bottom.
This troubling rift is at the heart of a recent editorial in Nature , titled "The Complex Truth About Trust in Science," as well as observations by African bioethics scholar Nchangwi Munung. Munung rightly reminds us that science succeeds only when scientists step out of their "ivory towers," listen to public concerns, engage society meaningfully, and speak candidly about scientific uncertainties.
In an age dominated by social media and an overwhelming "infodemic" of misinformation, uncovering the roots of this public skepticism is a vital necessity for safeguarding society.
Historically, the scientific community has often viewed the public through the lens of the "Knowledge Deficit Model" which assumes that people doubt science simply because they lack understanding and that pushing one-way information will automatically resolve skepticism.
However, modern science communication and social science have demonstrated that this assumption is not only flawed but counterproductive. Science is not a divine decree to be accepted blindly.
Public trust in science is not an institutional entitlement. It must be earned through integrity. This trust rests on three foundational pillars:
When scientific institutions position themselves as infallible or dismiss public fears, cultural nuances, and lived experiences as mere "unreason," they create a void that is quickly filled by misinformation and anti-science sentiments.
When scientific discourse remains confined to high-walled laboratories, paywalled journals, and dense academic jargon, it inevitably becomes alienated from society. This institutional elitism is one of science's greatest vulnerabilities. While public engagement is widely preached in theory, its practical implementation remains minimal.
Consider agricultural biotechnology or genome editing: While these tools hold immense potential for global food security, public skepticism will persist as long as researchers ignore farmers' local knowledge, economic anxieties, and lived realities.
To be truly effective, science must descend from its elevated pedestal and root itself in the soil of human experience.
While politics and religion frequently lay claim to absolute truths, science operates differently. Science states: "This is our best conclusion based on current evidence, but it remains open to revision as new data emerges."
Unfortunately, the public often misinterprets this inherent adaptability as hesitation or failure, a phenomenon vividly seen during the shifting health guidelines of the Covid-19 pandemic.
In reality, uncertainty is not a flaw in science; it is the engine of scientific progress.
If science had all the answers upfront, further inquiry would be redundant.
Communicating transparently about what we know, and what we have yet to discover, is the highest form of scientific honesty, and it is precisely what fosters long-term public trust.
The history of science demonstrates that during times of crisis, open science, open data, and international collaboration offer the fastest pathways to solutions.
When Bangladesh faced a devastating wheat blast outbreak in 2016, international researchers openly shared genomic data, leading to a swift diagnostic and management breakthrough. Similarly, open data sharing accelerated global responses during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Traditionally, locking research behind paywalls and hoarding data aligned science with corporate or geopolitical interests. In contrast, making data freely accessible allows researchers worldwide to conduct rigorous peer reviews, sharply reducing data manipulation and predatory practices.
Open science proves that scientific knowledge is not the private property of a few institutions or nations. It is a collective human heritage.
In today's digital landscape, we live amidst an unprecedented "infodemic," where conspiracy theories and sensationalist falsehoods spread far faster than scientific facts because they exploit human fear and emotion. Standard institutional press releases are no longer sufficient to counter this threat. To bridge this gap, scientists must adopt relatable metaphors and narrative-driven communication.
Simultaneously, we must expand citizen science initiatives, actively involving farmers, healthcare workers, teachers, and youth in data collection and problem-solving.
When a farmer sees that their field observations contributed directly to developing a disease-resistant crop or a rapid diagnostic kit, skepticism gives way to genuine ownership and trust.
Furthermore, academic institutions must invest in journalists by offering science communication fellowships and "media-meets-scientists" workshops, empowering them to translate complex topics into clear, accurate public narratives.
Science does not exist in a vacuum; it is deeply intertwined with public policy and ethics.
When policymakers misuse scientific claims to push political agendas, or when researchers compromise objectivity for corporate funding, public faith collapses.
Upholding rigorous ethical standards across all levels of scholarly communication is non-negotiable. Beyond disclosing conflicts of interest, the scientific community must actively combat the scourge of predatory journals and academic misconduct, such as data fabrication and plagiarism, which lead to damaging paper retractions.
Science can serve as a trusted guide only when it remains independent, ethically sound, and willing to publicly admit its errors.
Restoring public trust in science is not a one-off campaign; it requires an enduring institutional commitment. Embracing the principle of "science for society" means shifting our focus from merely accumulating citations in paywalled journals to driving real, positive social impact.
By breaking down the barriers of secrecy through open science and citizen science, and by communicating with clarity and humility, we can dismantle the ivory tower.
Science must no longer be viewed as an aloof, elite authority but as humanity’s most reliable, shared, and democratic instrument for navigating the uncertainties of the future.
Tofazzal Islam is Dean of Graduate Studies, and Founder Director and Professor at the Institute of Biotechnology and Genetic Engineering, Gazipur Agricultural University. Email: tofazzalislam@gau.edu.bd .

item.title: Rethinking waterlogging and flooding: Why our understanding matters. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On Sunday, 49mm of rain was recorded in Dhaka in nine hours that triggered widespread waterlogging in many parts of the city, causing disruptions to daily life and leaving commuters stranded.
Whenever there is flooding and waterlogging, we often see public frustration and criticism, indicating that this is a consequence of corruption, inadequate drainage networks, encroachment on wetlands and natural waterways, poor waste management, and unplanned urban expansion.
Many of these concerns are valid and should be reasonably addressed.
At the same time, we have to acknowledge that compared to the past, there have been improvements in infrastructural development -- and it is continuing.
Yet, why do we continue to face the same issues, sometimes even worse than before?
This is why our knowledge of climate change and its recent dynamics is also important to understand. Our widespread public perception is that economic development and improved infrastructure can eliminate these problems.
Investment in drainage systems, urban planning, and climate-resilient infrastructure is undoubtedly essential, but it is unrealistic to assume that development alone can completely shield cities from the forces of a rapidly changing climate.
Recent floods in some of the world's most developed cities indicate that even the best cities can be flooded and illustrate how rapid climate patterns are changing and challenging conventional planning assumptions.
On September 2, Toronto was hit by severe flooding after intense rainfall that overwhelmed drainage systems, disrupted transportation networks, and affected daily life.
On the same day, several cities in China's southeastern Fujian Province were inundated by torrential rains which were powerful enough to sweep away vehicles.
Similar flooding events have also been reported this year in New York City, Philadelphia, Washington DC, and Tokyo.
It shows that no city is immune to the growing risks of extreme weather. The fact that highly advanced and well-resourced cities continue to face devastating floods does not necessarily mean that their planning systems have failed.
Rather, it highlights a new reality: Many infrastructure systems designed using historical climate data have become obsolete.
Weather projections play a critical role in floodplain mapping and resilient infrastructure design. Yet at this time of history, climate projections are becoming increasingly difficult.
Hence, future development planning such as housing, roads, and bridges require a comprehensive understanding of climate change and its dynamics.
The recent Nepal disaster is a clear sign that climate related disasters can take shape in ways we never imagined possible. There is now this warning from the United Nations that natural climate phenomena such as El Niño may cause more extreme weather patterns such as droughts, flooding, extreme heat, and wildfires.
We are both a least developed country (LDC) and one of the world's most climate-vulnerable nations. Each year, millions of people are affected by climate-induced events, particularly during the four-to-five-month long monsoon season.
This year, the flooding in southern Chittagong, especially Banshkhali was a big shock to the local people who never imagined rainwater could trigger such a devastating flood situation in a coastal area.
If we only focus on governance and infrastructure failures, it will not be sufficient. Well-designed urban systems can and are overwhelmed by unprecedented volumes of rainfall and other climate-related shocks.
Thus, we should see flooding not only as an infrastructure challenge that can always be solved by engineering, but also as a rapidly changing climate challenge.
The assumption that every challenge can be permanently solved through human engineering or planning has created a false sense of stability for us.
In a world where environmental, social, and technological conditions are constantly changing, policies and long-term plans can become outdated more quickly than expected.
This is why climate education and awareness are an essential investment in our collective future. Climate education is not merely about acquiring knowledge, it is about preparing individuals, communities, and institutions to adapt to a world where environmental change is constant but uncertain.
Adaptation should not be viewed as a sign of weakness or failure. Rather, it is a practical and forward-looking strategy for navigating an uncertain future.
The goal is not to create systems that never fail, but to build societies that can learn, evolve, and respond effectively when conditions change.
Parvez Uddin Chowdhury is a development worker.

item.title: The court of public opinion and the iron bars of injustice. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
When Kamrunnahar Moni walked through the heavy gates of Kashimpur Women’s Central Jail, she did not step into freedom alone.
Holding her hand was her seven-year-old daughter, Mobashwera.
Seven years ago, in 2019, Moni was arrested while five months pregnant in connection with the tragic, horrifying murder of Nusrat Jahan Rafi in Sonagazi, Feni.
The nation, rightly heartbroken and outraged by Nusrat's death, demanded immediate, uncompromising justice.
But in that tempest of fury, public sentiment demanded heads, and the machinery of justice rushed to deliver them.
All 16 accused in the lower tribunal were handed down the death penalty. Among them was Moni, who subsequently gave birth inside a prison ward and raised her daughter behind bars.
The child’s early world was confined to high perimeter walls, where a schoolbag had to be fashioned out of torn cloth and dolls improvised from rolled-up socks.
Fast forward to the High Court’s recent verdict: Upon thorough re-evaluation of the evidence, ten individuals -- including Moni -- were acquitted after the court observed that charges against them were not proven beyond reasonable doubt.
In fact, the High Court went so far as to observe that the trial court judge had failed to apply necessary judicial consideration, blanket-sentencing all 16 to death without individually evaluating their role or degree of involvement.
Moni and her child are now free, but what restores seven lost years? What heals a childhood spent inside a condemnation cell?
The tragedy of Moni’s stolen youth is not merely an institutional error; it is a stark, haunting reminder of what happens when societal bloodlust and media trials dictate the trajectory of justice.
A media trial occurs when popular perception, amplified by television studios, sensationalist headlines, and digital mobs, constructs a narrative of guilt long before a court of law evaluates a single exhibit.
When a shocking crime occurs, the public craves swift retribution.
Media outlets, driven by ratings and social media algorithms that monetize outrage, willingly feed this appetite.
In this echo chamber, nuanced legal thresholds like "presumption of innocence" and "proof beyond reasonable doubt" are discarded as inconvenient technicalities.
Suspects are tried, convicted, and vilified on television and viral Facebook posts within hours of an arrest.
The danger lies in how this manufactured public consensus permeates the wider environment.
It creates an oppressive atmosphere where investigating agencies feel immense pressure to produce immediate results, leading to rushed charge sheets, forced confessions, and compromised evidence gathering.
Judges, though bound by law, are human beings living in the same society; when an entire country is baying for blood, exercising judicial restraint and demanding strict evidentiary standards requires extraordinary fortitude.
Yet, from an evidentiary standpoint, public outrage and media commentary are completely inadmissible in a court of law.
A judge cannot convict an individual because a million people on social media believe they are guilty.
Justice must be anchored in vetted testimony, cross-examined witnesses, and physical, verifiable proof.
When public perception usurps this process, the legal system ceases to be an instrument of justice and becomes a court of public satisfaction.
The tragedy of the Nusrat trial is far from an isolated incident in Bangladesh's legal history.
The public consciousness is littered with cases where initial media frenzies built airtight narratives of guilt, only for those narratives to collapse years later under rigorous legal scrutiny.
Consider the sensational 2012 double murder of journalist couple Sagar Sarowar and Meherun Runi.
For years, media speculation ran wild, leaking unverified police theories, painting suspects in vivid strokes of guilt, and distracting from core forensic shortcomings.
Over a decade and dozens of probe deadline extensions later, the case remains a glaring testament to how noise and media commentary often obscure the search for genuine truth.
Similarly, in high-profile homicide or narcotics cases, the immediate public parade of accused individuals before television cameras -- often before formal charges are framed -- destroys reputations beyond repair.
Even when higher courts eventually acquit these individuals due to lack of evidence, the media rarely covers the acquittal with the same fervor it gave to the arrest.
The public remembers the accused as a monster; the quiet, dignified legal exoneration years later is buried on page seven.
The fundamental flaw of trial by media is that it demands speed over accuracy. But speed in law often leads to irreversible tragedy.
When a society prioritizes catharsis over due process, it creates a system where an innocent pregnant woman can be swept into a blanket death sentence, forced to nurse her newborn in a condemned cell while the public moves on to the next headline.
Seven years of Mobashwera’s life were lived in incarceration not because she committed a crime, but because the initial judicial process rushed to satisfy a collective demand for total retribution.
Public sentiment is erratic, emotional, and easily manipulated; it does not weigh evidence, cross-examine motives, or protect the vulnerable.
The court of law was specifically designed to act as a barrier against the volatile whims of the public square.
It exists precisely to ensure that even amid the most horrific tragedies, the innocent are not sacrificed to appease the mob.
As a society, we must confront our role in these structural failures.
Media outlets must exercise ethical restraint, resisting the temptation to play judge, jury, and executioner for clicks.
Law enforcement agencies must cease performing investigations through press briefings.
Most importantly, as citizens, we must learn to separate our legitimate grief and anger over a crime from our demand for legal process.
Justice is not served when we send 16 people to the gallows simply to feel that a wrong has been righted.
Real justice demands precision, patience, and adherence to law -- because when rash judgment takes over, the innocent pay the price, and their stolen years can never be returned.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Give peace a chance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the world marks the International Day of Peace under the United Nations theme “Invest in Peace: For Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day,” the global landscape today is, to say the least, fractured.
Global leaders gathering for the 81st UN General Assembly face an international order that has been left reeling by persistent conflicts, severe economic disruption, and an accelerating climate crisis that threatens vulnerable nations first.
True peace extends beyond the mere signing of accords or temporary ceasefires. For a nation such as ours, it requires building resilient social foundations.
Investing in peace means channeling resources into conflict resolution, strengthening democratic institutions, and safeguarding human rights. Crucially, it also means addressing the socioeconomic inequities that fuel unrest.
In a year that looks increasingly like one defined by wars and global inflation alike, security and justice remain indispensable pillars of lasting stability.
However, given environmental degradation and economic challenges such as persistent and crippling inflation, in addition to energy crises, peace also means economic security and climate justice.
When communities lack basic security, clean water, or economic opportunity, social cohesion inevitably crumbles.
For Bangladesh, investing in peace begins at home and extends to our regional responsibilities.
Domestically in particular, it requires fostering inclusive dialogue, upholding the rule of law, and ensuring that economic progress leaves no citizen behind. Regionally, it demands renewed international pressure to resolve the Rohingya crisis -- a protracted displacement that burdens our national resources and threatens regional stability.
Peace is not a passive state, nor can it be achieved solely in international conference rooms. It is an active, day-to-day commitment by governments, civil society, and citizens alike.
On this International Day of Peace, world leaders must move beyond performative pledges to build a world where peace is guaranteed for everyone, everywhere, every day.

item.title: Zero tolerance for stoking public fear. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Over the past few days, our country looks to have plunged back into an atmosphere of anxiety and dread.
A relentless wave of synchronized arson attacks and crude bomb explosions, targeting public transports to bustling hubs alike, is nothing if not a direct, malicious assault on the public’s sense of safety.
It goes without saying that these acts of sabotage must be unequivocally condemned by every segment of society.
There is no political objective or grievance that justifies throwing crude bombs into crowded public areas or setting commuter buses ablaze. It is important that every single person in this country recognizes this.
When terrified passengers are forced to flee burning buses, or pedestrians running about in panic as a result of the crude bombs, it is innocent civilians who bear the brunt of this violence.
These are not and have never been acts of political expression. They must be identified for what they are: Lawless acts of terror designed to instill fear, disrupt public life, and destabilize the state.
While the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s deployment of additional checkpoints and increased intelligence presence are necessary steps, reactive measures alone will not suffice.
What we need is for the authorities to deliver a swift, decisive response to identify, apprehend, and prosecute every individual involved -- from those hurling explosives and setting the vehicles on fire on the ground to those orchestrating these attacks from behind the scenes.
The state has a fundamental duty to guarantee the basic safety and freedom of movement of the public, and the citizens of this country cannot be left to navigate their daily lives under the shadow of violence.
Lawlessness must be met with an unyielding zero-tolerance policy. Nothing else will do.

item.description:
In the first week of September, 38 Bangladeshis returned home from Cambodia, some rescued from cyber scam compounds and others unable to return after travelling there for work. They were not the first. A few months earlier, 583 Bangladeshis had returned from Cambodia, while around 1,800 more were reportedly waiting to come home.
According to Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training data cited in recent reports, 15,921 Bangladeshis travelled to Cambodia for employment over the previous year and a half. When returns occur on this scale, they are difficult to treat simply as isolated migration failures.
One returnee from Lakshmipur reportedly paid Tk 5.3 lakh for what he was told would be a computer operator's job. He obtained BMET clearance before departure, but after reaching Cambodia discovered that he had travelled on a one month visit visa.
He alleged that Bangladeshi brokers received him at the airport and eventually handed him over to a cyber scam compound. The case raises a question that awareness campaigns alone cannot answer: If a worker can pass through a formal emigration process while the visa does not correspond with the employment promised, where did verification fail?
Cambodia represents one form of migration-related exploitation, but recent developments elsewhere reveal different dimensions of the problem. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, 36 Bangladeshis were among migrants intercepted in two alleged irregular crossing attempts near the Croatian border.
Meanwhile, the better known route through Libya and the Mediterranean continues to involve irregular movement, detention, deaths at sea, and repatriation. On September 1 alone, another 174 Bangladeshis returned from a Libyan detention centre.
These cases should not be treated as identical. Human trafficking, migrant smuggling, deceptive labour recruitment, and irregular migration involve different circumstances and legal questions. Yet they reveal a common governance challenge: By the time a migrant is exploited in a destination country, detained along an irregular route, or rescued and repatriated, several earlier stages of the migration process have already passed.
The policy question therefore begins before rescue or return. It concerns how recruitment practices are verified, how emerging risks are identified, and whether lessons from previous cases influence decisions about future migration.
Returnee experiences can provide an important source of evidence for prevention. When similar problems involving recruiters, agencies, visas, job offers, or destinations appear across multiple cases, they may indicate weaknesses in the recruitment process rather than isolated individual failures. Systematically identifying these patterns could help authorities investigate emerging risks and strengthen verification before more workers are affected.
The Cambodia cases make this particularly relevant. Authorities can examine what jobs were promised, how much workers paid, what visas they received, whether they obtained emigration clearance, which agencies or intermediaries were involved, and how recruitment took place. If the same visa discrepancy, recruiter, agency, or recruitment method repeatedly appears, that information should inform investigation and future clearance decisions.
The need for such learning is becoming more urgent as recruitment itself changes. Cyber scam compounds show how exploitation can initially resemble legitimate employment.
Jobs may be presented as computer operator, customer service, or call centre positions, while communication takes place through familiar digital platforms. The deception may become clear only after the worker reaches the destination.
This means prevention cannot depend only on telling prospective migrants to be careful. It also requires institutions to recognize changing recruitment patterns and make reliable verification accessible before departure.
Bangladesh already has institutions responsible for different parts of migration governance. The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and BMET regulate important aspects of labour migration. Bangladesh missions abroad encounter problems affecting citizens at destination, while the Ministry of Home Affairs, police, immigration, and investigative agencies deal with trafficking, migrant smuggling and organised criminal networks.
The challenge is ensuring that information moves effectively between them. The migrant passes through one journey, not several institutional mandates. Information gathered from a returnee may be relevant to an investigation, a recruiting agency's record, a future clearance decision, a diplomatic mission, and another person considering the same job or destination. If these pieces remain disconnected, each institution may see only one part of the problem.
A more preventive system would therefore connect evidence from returnees, complaints, visa, and clearance records, recruiting agencies, overseas missions, and investigations. This does not require assuming that every unsuccessful migration experience indicates trafficking or institutional failure. It means looking for repeated patterns early enough to determine whether intervention is necessary.
The importance of doing so becomes clearer when these cases are considered alongside Bangladesh's remittance performance. The country received a record $35.5 billion in remittances in fiscal year 2025 to 2026, about 17.3% more than the previous year. The economic contribution of migrant workers is beyond dispute.
But a migration system should not be assessed only by the number of workers who leave or the remittances they eventually send home. Its capacity to identify questionable recruitment, verify employment pathways, detect emerging forms of exploitation, and intervene before harm occurs is equally important.
NGOs and international organizations have important roles in awareness, community engagement, referrals, survivor assistance, and reintegration. Yet there are limits to what project-based interventions can do.
An awareness session cannot authenticate a foreign employer, examine patterns across thousands of visas, regulate a recruiting agency, investigate financial transactions or prosecute an organized network. These functions require institutional authority and coordination.
This is why repeated returns should be understood as more than repatriation events. The 38 Bangladeshis returning from Cambodia, together with hundreds who returned earlier, may provide information about where recruitment safeguards failed.
Bangladeshis intercepted in Bosnia raise different questions about the networks and decisions that brought them onto irregular routes in Europe. Repeated detention and return from Libya can similarly provide evidence about established pathways and intermediaries.
The purpose is neither to portray every migrant as a helpless victim nor to place responsibility entirely on institutions.
Migrants exercise agency, but their decisions are made within recruitment systems and information environments that they cannot independently regulate or verify. Effective migration governance must recognize both realities.
For a country receiving more than $35bn a year from its citizens abroad, bringing people home after exploitation or irregular migration is necessary, but it should not be the end of the response.
The more important test is whether what Bangladesh learns from those who return can prevent the next migrant from facing the same experience.
Md Shihabul Hossain works on irregular migration, human trafficking, and migrant reintegration issues with Brac’s migration program. The views expressed are personal.

item.title: The hyper-commercialization of therapy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For the overwhelming span of human history, the architecture of emotional survival rested upon rather unglamorous but formidable institutions: Family, friendship, faith, philosophy, and community.
Human beings grieved, failed, lost fortunes, endured betrayal, and buried those they loved without automatically interpreting every emotional upheaval as a pathology requiring professional intervention.
Suffering was not romanticized, but neither was it medicalized; it was understood as one of the immutable vicissitudes of the human condition.
Stoicism, Buddhism, classical philosophy, and religious traditions offered frameworks through which people learned to distinguish adversity from annihilation, and pain from permanent defeat.
Epictetus urged his followers to differentiate between what lies within our control and what does not; Marcus Aurelius repeatedly reminded himself that external events cannot be governed, but one’s response to them can; Aristotle understood character as something cultivated through habit rather than bestowed by circumstance.
Yet the social architecture that once absorbed much of our anguish has progressively frayed beneath hyper-individualism, urban isolation, and the atomization of modern life.
Into that vacuum has emerged a formidable commercial apparatus in which therapy, wellness, self-help, and psychological language have become lucrative commodities.
Modern clinical talk therapy began in the late 19th and early 20th centuries with Sigmund Freud’s development of psychoanalysis. Insurance and corporate integrated by the 1970s and 1980s, and corporations began buying therapy services in bulk to protect workplace productivity.
What was once principally a specialized clinical intervention has, through media romanticism, influencer culture, and subscription-based telehealth, acquired the trappings of lifestyle consumption.
The pertinent question is therefore not whether therapy works. It unquestionably can, and evidence-based psychotherapy has an important place in treating genuine psychological disorders.
The more disquieting question is whether capitalism has discovered how to commodify ordinary human suffering, cultivate perpetual emotional insecurity, and then sell us an ostensibly indispensable remedy.
The therapy industry has attracted massive backing from high-profile venture capital and private equity firms. According to Precedence Research, the global behavioral health market size is valued at $184.94 billion for 2025 and is projected to hit $197.34 billion by 2026. Over the next decade, this upward trajectory is set to skyrocket.
Capitalism has long perfected a familiar stratagem: Manufacture an insecurity, amplify it, then monetize the cure. We now inhabit an economy in which there appears to be a pharmaceutical answer for every mood and a corrective procedure for every perceived bodily deficiency: Sad, anxious, confused, sleepless, heartbroken, exhausted, distracted, down. There is a pill, program, subscription, or product waiting to intervene.
The same commercial logic has colonized the female body, persuading women that virtually every visible imperfection requires rectification until women across the globe are subtly conscripted into pursuing the same homogenized beauty ideal, a real-life Barbie manufactured by advertising rather than biology.
Wrinkles must disappear, bodies must be sculpted, aging must be resisted, skin must be altered, and every deviation from an algorithmically-approved aesthetic treated as a defect.
In this relentless pursuit of optimization, we have forgotten one of the most elemental tenets of being human: Beauty resides partly in its flaws.
A scar has history; a wrinkle has chronology; grief is evidence that something mattered. The perfectly engineered body and the perfectly regulated emotional life may be commercially desirable, but neither is necessarily synonymous with human flourishing.
Therapy-speak represents the psychological counterpart of this same phenomenon. Clinical terminology, once possessing precise diagnostic meaning has migrated into social media vernacular, where disagreement becomes “gaslighting,” selfishness becomes “narcissism,” an agonizing breakup becomes “trauma,” and difficult relatives become “toxic.”
“Boundaries” can be a salutary instrument of self-respect, yet the phrase can equally camouflage avoidance, emotional immaturity, or an unwillingness to reconcile. “Protecting my peace” can signify wisdom, but it can also become a fashionable alibi for abandoning every relationship that demands patience, accountability, or reciprocal compromise.
Even “trauma bond,” a term describing a severe psychological attachment between an abused person and an abuser, is routinely misappropriated online to describe ordinary intimacy forged through shared hardship.
The danger is not that people possess a richer vocabulary for emotional life; it is that vocabulary becomes verdict, diagnosis becomes identity, and ordinary human friction is recast as pathology.
The gap between the media's romanticized version of therapy and the lived reality of consumers has left many feeling profoundly let down and financially drained.
“At first, it felt incredible to vent. But after months passed, I realized my therapist wasn't actually giving me tools to move on; she was just agreeing with me every week.
“I spent over $5,000 to essentially rent a supportive friend for 50 minutes a week. When I tried to bring up ending our sessions, she subtly suggested I had deeper, repressed childhood trauma I wasn't ready to face. I felt manipulated into staying dependent just to keep her schedule filled."
"My therapist actively encouraged me to set rigid boundaries and cut out 'toxic energy' over minor family disagreements. I did it, thinking it was the ultimate sign of emotional maturity.
“Two years later, I woke up completely isolated. I had no real-world community left -- only a therapist I had to pay to talk to. The process stripped away my natural support systems under the guise of self-care."
This is where our modern proclivity for the quick fix becomes particularly revealing. We prefer diet pills to disciplined habits, cosmetic intervention to reconciliation with aging, instant gratification to deferred fulfillment, and algorithms to contemplation.
Therapy can become another manifestation of this consumer instinct when paying for emotional assistance begins to substitute for cultivating the internal faculties required to confront life.
Reading, building character, doing meditation or prayers, sustaining difficult friendships, tolerating ambiguity, accepting loss, and assuming responsibility are arduous enterprises; there is no subscription button for them.
A weekly appointment, by contrast, can create the comforting sensation that one is doing something profound merely because one is paying someone to listen.
Yet, genuine therapy should not become an infinite paid friendship. A responsible therapeutic relationship ought to have professional boundaries, meaningful objectives, and an orientation towards greater autonomy.
When a practitioner discourages termination indefinitely, continually discovers ever-deeper “repressed” explanations whenever progress is questioned, or deploys terminology such as “resistance,” “defensiveness” or “transference” to deflect legitimate concerns about cost or efficacy, the clinical vocabulary itself can become a shield.
The danger of transference is real, but so is the possibility of dependency. A person who gradually abandons friends, family, and community because every difficult relationship is labelled toxic may discover, years later, that the only dependable person left in their emotional ecosystem is someone they must pay by the hour.
The irony is almost Kafkaesque: The disintegration of community creates loneliness; loneliness creates demand for professional companionship; professional companionship becomes commercialized; and the consumer is then encouraged to remain sufficiently psychologically unfinished to sustain the transaction.
We should therefore recover something that modern education has largely relegated to the margins: Practical philosophy. Imagine a curriculum in which children are not merely instructed how to pass examinations but how to inhabit a human life.
A young student could encounter Epictetus through one deceptively simple question: What is within my control? Marcus Aurelius could introduce the discipline of responding rather than reacting. Aristotle could teach that character is constituted through repeated habits, prompting students to examine which daily behaviours are shaping the person they are becoming. Socrates could teach intellectual humility by asking: How do I know what I believe is true?
Buddhist philosophy could introduce impermanence, attachment and the acceptance of change. Viktor Frankl could ask what gives suffering meaning rather than merely how to abolish discomfort.
Students could maintain reflection journals, distinguish fact from interpretation, practise conflict resolution, learn delayed gratification, examine consumer manipulation, discuss grief and mortality, and learn how to disagree without immediately severing relationships.
Adolescents could study digital addiction, loneliness, rejection, friendship, responsibility, and the psychology of persuasion.
Such education would not diminish psychiatry or psychotherapy; paradoxically, it could make society more discerning about when professional intervention is genuinely warranted.
Someone experiencing severe depression, debilitating anxiety, or another clinical disorder should not be told to meditate their way out of illness.
Professional treatment can be indispensable. But neither should every disappointment be elevated into trauma, every sadness into pathology or every interpersonal disagreement into abuse. The wisdom lies in distinguishing illness from adversity, and vulnerability from incapacity.
Perhaps the greatest casualty of hyper-commercialized emotional culture is our faith in our own capacity to endure. Previous generations were hardly paragons of psychological health; many suffered in silence when they needed professional help, and we should not romanticize deprivation simply because it was endured without a therapist.
Yet they often possessed an implicit understanding that life itself is an apprenticeship in loss. We should not discard that inheritance merely because modern psychology has given us better tools. We should integrate the two.
Therapy should be available when clinically necessary, but it should not become a lifestyle brand; medicine should treat illness without manufacturing endless insecurity; communities should become sufficiently cohesive that loneliness is not automatically monetized; families should recover their function as places of refuge; and schools should teach young people not merely what to think, but how to cope, deliberate, reconcile, recover, and remain intellectually sovereign.
Marcus Aurelius and Viktor Frankl arrived at their conclusions through radically different worlds, yet both recognized a proposition that contemporary consumer culture finds inconvenient: Circumstances will forever remain partly beyond our jurisdiction, but the cultivation of character is not.
The antidote to an economy that profits from our fragility is not to reject therapy, medicine, or modern psychology, but to refuse the proposition that every discomfort requires a product.
We need neither stoic indifference nor therapeutic dependence. We need resilience with discernment, community without suffocation, medicine without commodified insecurity, and a culture capable of telling the truth about suffering: sometimes it requires treatment; sometimes it requires companionship; sometimes it requires philosophy; sometimes surrendering to God, prayers, and meditation; and sometimes, painfully and beautifully, it simply requires time.
Alisha Pradhan is Founder, HerNet Foundation and HerNet TV.

item.title: China swim sensation, 13, sets Asian Games record after Japan win early. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi set an Asian Games record as she scorched to gold on Sunday’s first full day of competition, after hosts Japan celebrated early success.

The first gold medal of the 20th edition of the two-week multi-sport extravaganza went to Japan’s Takumi Hojo in the men’s individual triathlon.

In the evening, it was over to Yu as the schoolgirl who turns 14 next month took the women’s 200m butterfly crown in a Games-record 2min 05.08sec.

It was the first major title of her young career, less than two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics.

“It was only so-so,” a smiling Yu said after receiving her medal, warning she can go faster yet.

Yu became the youngest medallist in swimming world championships history last year when she took home relay bronze aged 12.

Swimming is one of three sports at the Games taking place in Tokyo, where a typhoon is due to blow in, with the rest of the Games unfolding in Nagoya and Aichi prefecture.

China are expected to be the preeminent power in the pool, and they showed why on day one as they clinched six of the seven titles on the night.

‘Beautiful’

The Games were declared open on Saturday by Emperor Naruhito, but there were a large number of empty seats at the 30,000-capacity stadium in Nagoya.

It sounded the starting pistol on a fortnight of intense action as the continent’s finest athletes compete in more than 40 sports before the curtain comes down on October 4.

The Games have 2028 Olympic places up for grabs but have been dogged by a series of problems in the build-up.

Accommodating the more than 11,000 athletes and 6,000 officials has stretched organisers to the limit after they decided not to have a traditional athletes’ village to save money.

Competitors instead are staying in a combination of temporary container-style huts, hotels and on the Costa Serena cruise ship.

IOC president Kirsty Coventry called the temporary huts “beautiful” on Sunday after having a look round — but conceded they were “a little tighter” than similar accommodation at the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics this year.

Typhoon threat

Japanese organisers will be desperate for the sport to take over from a troubled lead-in that included complaints about the accommodation and a shortage of rooms.

However, an incoming typhoon that soaked Tokyo on Sunday could cause more problems.

The Tokyo venue hosting equestrian was closed because of the weather.

The competition is now due to start on Tuesday, a day later than originally planned.

Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain Al-Musallam said the typhoon threat was part of the reason why there were thousands of empty seats at the opening ceremony.

The full force of Typhoon Dujuan won’t be felt until Monday, with Tokyo expected to be hit with strong winds and heavy rain.

Nagoya won’t be in the storm’s immediate path, but wet weather is forecast there too.

Emotional Iran bronze

Iran celebrated wildly after beating China 79-70 to win men’s basketball bronze.

“I think after the obstacles that we faced since six months ago, we proved everybody wrong again,” forward Arsalan Kazemi said in reference to the Middle East war.

South Korea won basketball gold, silencing the home crowd with a 67-57 win over Japan.

Launching the day’s action, the hosts’ triathlete Hojo finished the 750m swim, 20km bike ride and 5,000m run in 52min 56sec, nine seconds clear of China’s Zhang Xirui.

In other sports, Smriti Mandhana became the highest run-scorer in women’s T20 international cricket as India crushed Bangladesh by 114 runs in the semi-finals, with fellow opener Shafali Verma hitting her maiden hundred.

Mandhana scored 37 off 19 balls and went past New Zealand all-rounder Suzie Bates’s 4,758 runs at the top of the all-time list.

India will face Sri Lanka in Tuesday’s final, unless the weather intervenes.

item.title: Humanizing our prisons. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The crisis unfolding across the prison system in Chittagong is a stark reminder of a structural failure that can no longer be ignored.
Facilities designed to hold a combined capacity of 7,892 inmates are currently housing nearly 20,000 prisoners -- more than two and a half times what they were built to accommodate. At Chittagong Central Jail alone, 6,903 individuals are packed into a space meant for 2,249.
This severe deficit in physical capacity undermines the fundamental purpose of correctional institutions and violates basic human dignity.
When prisoners receive less than a fraction of the mandated living space, and when two or three inmates are routinely squeezed into berths meant for one, sanitation, health, and security rapidly deteriorate.
Worse still, space constraints prevent authorities from separating prisoners by legal status or the severity of their offenses. Placing petty offenders and pre-trial detainees alongside hardened convicts converts correctional spaces into breeding grounds for criminal networks rather than centres for rehabilitation.
Addressing this crisis requires immediate, multi-pronged intervention. While building additional facilities is a necessary long-term step, structural expansion alone will not solve the issue.
The judicial system must also expedite pre-trial proceedings and expand the use of bail for non-violent, minor offenses to relieve pressure on overcrowded cells.
Imprisonment was never meant to strip people of basic human decency. Treating inmates humanely is not a concession but an obligation, and is a reflection of civil society.
We expect the government to recognize the scale of the issue and take the necessary steps to allocate sufficient resources to expand prison capacity, modernize infrastructure, and enforce more humane living standards across all of our correctional facilities.

item.title: The real wall blocking the Bimstec free trade agreement. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Ask most analysts why the Bimstec FTA has gone nowhere since 2004, and you get one answer: Politics. Big powers can't agree, small states feel pushed around, and even after eight rounds of negotiation, the agreement remains far from finalizing their agreements.
But this article makes a sharper claim. Even if every Bimstec leader signed the agreement tomorrow, trade would barely move. The deeper problem isn't political will. It's the sheer unevenness of customs systems, product standards, and border infrastructure across the region. This is a regulatory problem, not a diplomatic one, and it needs a different fix.
The conventional account has real evidence behind it. The framework agreement was signed in 2004, but two decades later, its six parts, covering goods, services, investment, customs, trade facilitation, and dispute settlement, remain unfinished.
Bimstec's own Secretary-General has called the FTA's progress "very slow," and said member states are now considering finalizing only the parts closest to agreement instead of waiting for the whole package.
But this explanation has a problem. It can't explain why trade stays low even in product categories where tariffs are already fairly low, and even between countries with decent relations.
If politics were the whole story, trade should flow more easily where diplomacy is warmest. That isn't what happens. Something else is keeping goods stuck at the border.
It also can't explain why other regional blocs with their own share of political tension, such as Asean, still manage to trade far more with each other.
Look past the negotiating table and toward the customs shed, and the picture becomes clearer. The trade numbers are damning on their own.
Intra-Bimstec trade stood at 6.7% of members' total trade in 2023, translating into regional trade worth $53.49 billion, up from $46 billion in 2019. For a bloc that includes India, one of the world's largest economies, this is strikingly small.
The region's own data shows why. The Asian Development Bank's 2022 trade facilitation framework grades each country's customs systems against WTO standards. Thailand and India report 91.6% and 72.3% full compliance, with no procedures stuck in the weakest category. Myanmar, by contrast, has only 5.5% full compliance, with 85.3% still in the weakest category. Nepal fares similarly poorly, at just 2.1% full compliance.
This isn't a picture of political disagreement. It's a picture of infrastructure and staffing running at completely different speeds across the same trade bloc.
This unevenness costs real time and money at the border. A monitoring study of one Bangladesh trade corridor found that completing routine trade procedures took roughly half a month for an experienced trader, and 18 days for a new trader. Border crossing alone took over six hours for imports.
On a single 455-kilometre corridor, cargo trucks spent close to 30 hours in transit, over 11 of which were pure waiting time. These delays are not just an inconvenience for traders. They add directly to the final price of goods, which makes Bimstec-made products less competitive even inside their own region
And the type of barrier matters most. Sanitary and technical standards, rules on food safety, product testing, and certification, they all add up. These aren't simple paperwork checks. Smaller exporters struggle to meet them because compliance needs functioning testing labs, which many border regions simply don't have. When a country lacks a certified lab near its crossing point, an otherwise reasonable safety rule turns into an impassable barrier.
Put together, these threads tell a clear story. Bimstec's economies aren't only failing to agree on paper, they're also failing to converge in practice also.
Thailand's digitized customs system has almost nothing in common with Bhutan's land-port capacity. A signature cannot paper over that gap. It has to be built into the agreement itself, through shared testing facilities, mutual recognition of standards, and real technical assistance for the countries furthest behind.
Bimstec's own strategy documents admit this is still missing, noting that without mutual recognition agreements, exporters face costly duplicate testing every time a product crosses a new border.
This isn't just an argument over labels. It changes where Bimstec should spend its effort. If the problem were mainly political, the fix would be more summits and leader-level trust-building. But if the deeper problem is regulatory unevenness, summits are the wrong tool.
What's actually needed is slower, less visible technical work such as joint investment in border testing labs, mutual recognition agreements, harmonized paperwork, and dedicated funding for Myanmar, Nepal, and Bhutan, which remain decades behind on digitized border systems.
There's reason to think this shift is already happening inside the bloc. Officials have floated splitting the FTA into components and finalizing the parts closest to completion instead of waiting for the whole agreement at once. That is, in effect, an admission that the technical layer, not the political layer, is where real progress can happen fastest.
Bimstec's stalled FTA is usually told as a story about mistrust between governments. That story isn't false, but it's incomplete.
The data points to a different diagnosis: The region's real wall is regulatory, built from mismatched testing labs, uneven digitization, and standards nobody has agreed to recognize across borders.
Political summits will not fix this. Only steady, long-term work on fixing these rules and systems will. Until Bimstec makes that a top priority, its free trade agreement can’t boost trade alone.
Sachin Yadav, PhD scholar in International Studies, Jamia Hamdard University, New Delhi.

item.title: How can we tax?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We can say that some sorts of taxation are unfair. VAT, for example, weighs more heavily upon the poor than it does the rich.
We might therefore say that we should have more income tax and less VAT to make the system fairer: The rich will be carrying more of the tax burden that way.
Or perhaps we should tax profit, or companies, or dividends, or all the other things we could be doing.
This is the background to the report by Supro and Oxfam Bangladesh that the VAT system is regressive. Regressive in this sense means something specific. More of a poor person's income goes in this tax than the percentage of a rich person's. The report says 12.1% in a poor household compared to 5.9% in a rich one.
A progressive tax would reverse that, a progressive tax gets more of a rich income than it does of a poor one.
So, if we were to run the tax system purely on the grounds of fairness, then we'd change that system.
And that it should be the richer paying for society is an entirely fair idea. Even Adam Smith said that taxes should be “more than in proportion” to income -- the richer pay more of their income as a percentage than the poorer.
But there's something else here as well. That fairness is also called “equity,” and we do not only run the tax system on equity. We also have to include efficiency.
With taxation sometimes, this just means how easy it is to collect the money. How many bureaucrats we have to pay to get the cash. But there's another meaning as well and it's an important one.
Whatever we tax, we get less of. If we tax profits, then fewer people go into business to try to make profits. If we tax building houses, then fewer houses will be built. Tax incomes and some people will just not work so hard.
But how much less we get depends upon what the tax is. How much less business -- or houses, or work -- we get is called the “deadweight cost” of the tax. The things that just do not happen because we have decided to have this tax.
Yes, we do have to have tax. It's also true that the tax we raise can be used to do wonderful things. But it is still true that we get less of whatever we tax and so these deadweight costs exist.
We know the spectrum as well. It is land taxes, consumption, income, capital and profits, transactions. There are also sin taxes -- alcohol, tobacco and so on, but there, we're actually trying to make people do less, so that's not quite relevant.
No one is making more land so taxing it doesn't mean less of it. But as we start moving through consumption -- VAT is the obvious tax here -- to income taxes, corporate and capital gains taxes, then those deadweight costs rise. We lose more in economic activity that just does not happen for each same amount of tax revenue we collect.
Which gives us a problem. Yes, we can design a tax system which is fair and equitable. This would mean making the rich pay for everything out of their profits and high incomes.
But this tax system would be inefficient -- we'd be losing more business, more jobs, more development, if we tried to do it this way.
We could also just say darn to fairness and pay for everything from land taxes. There's actually a whole school of economics, Georgism, devoted to that very idea.
That also wouldn't raise very much which would mean we'd need a VAT as well which is the unfairness we noted up top.
The sad thing here is that there's no solution to this problem. No solution within economics that is. Whether you think we should be fair at the cost of inefficiency, or efficient but unfair, is something from morals, not economics.
You bring your ideas -- ideals -- of morals to economics but economics cannot tell you what the correct morals are.
Which leaves us with that little problem. Yes, we can make the tax system fairer. In doing so, we'll make it less efficient and make the future poorer.
So, just what is the right balance?
The only right answer is that this is a choice we have got to make.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Ensuring megaprojects deliver. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council’s (ECNEC) recent approval of the MRT Line-5 (Southern) and the cost revisions for MRT Line-1 and Line-5 (Northern) -- totaling an extraordinary Tk 2.5 lakh crore -- tells us that Bangladesh remains committed to expanding its urban infrastructure.
There is, of course, nothing wrong with this. Expanding mass transit is undoubtedly essential to relieve the capital city’s crushing congestion.
Yet, allocating capital on this unprecedented scale demands absolute financial accountability, meticulous execution, and a guarantee that every taka spent delivers direct, tangible improvements to daily life.
Mega-infrastructure projects in Bangladesh have historically suffered from a familiar set of systemic vulnerabilities: Frequent implementation delays, extensive cost overruns, and administrative bottlenecks.
When project budgets balloon, the public rightfully demands transparency into why original estimates fell short. External loans from foreign partners like Japan and the Asian Development Bank must be repaid by taxpayers; therefore, cost escalation, which has unfortunately become standard operating procedure, cannot remain the norm for how our nation functions.
Prudent financial management must go beyond initial approvals and funding arrangements. The relevant leadership and project authorities must implement rigorous oversight mechanisms, strict project timelines, and transparent auditing process from inception to delivery.
Ultimately, infrastructure is only as good as the benefit it brings to average citizens. A multi-billion-dollar metro network should not merely serve as a symbol of modernity -- it must translate into safer commutes, reduced traffic bottlenecks, improved air quality, and predictable travel times across the capital.
Large-scale public investment requires equally large-scale discipline. If we continue to fail in our management of these funds, and if inefficiency continues to be our status quo, the risk of unsustainable fiscal pressure will overshadow the very benefits these megaprojects are intended to bring.
