item.title: Why Pakistan needs administrative restructuring. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan’s administrative map is carrying a population load it was never designed for. We are now a country of more than 240 million people.

Punjab alone is home to over 127 million people, Sindh more than 55 million and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa over 40 million. These numbers matter beyond being a headcount from a census. They help decide how far the government has to reach, how many people local institutions must serve, how development funds are shared and how fast the state can act.

Yet the spaces where political power, financial decisions and government action are concentrated remain very few. At the national level, Pakistan has only 266 directly elected National Assembly seats for a population of 241.5 million, averaging roughly one directly elected representative for every 908,000 people.

Overtly concentrated

Government is heavily concentrated in Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar and Quetta. Ministries, senior bureaucracies, large hospitals, universities, courts and development authorities gather around provincial capitals. Over time, economic activity follows them, as do jobs, professional services, infrastructure and investment. Such concentration has consequences for regions farther away.

A citizen in southern Punjab experiences provincial government differently from someone in Lahore. The same holds for Hazara in relation to Peshawar, or for distant districts in Sindh and Balochistan. Geography eventually becomes administrative distance. Files move through longer chains, senior decision-makers remain elsewhere and development priorities compete for attention with those of much larger metropolitan centres. This is exactly why the debate over new administrative units deserves to be linked directly with prosperity.

In economics, government exerts a gravitational pull. A centre of administration creates surrounding departments, courts, universities, hospitals, infrastructure, housing, services and jobs, and this draws businesses towards it. It also fosters professional communities; roads are built or improved, land prices rise and new markets form. All these dynamics can be seen across Pakistan around existing provincial capitals. There is, therefore, no real reason to assume that the same institutional pull would not help build additional regional growth centres.

South Punjab is an obvious example of this administrative logic. The establishment of the South Punjab Secretariat in 2020 acknowledged the problem caused by placing all authority in Lahore. One of its stated purposes was to allow people in the area to have their issues resolved closer to where they live. This recognition was important because it accepted that proximity to government has both economic and social value.

Similarly, Hazara has demanded a separate province for many years. In August 2026, proponents again linked the demand with demographic growth, governance and administrative feasibility. Previously, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Assembly had adopted resolutions in favour of a separate province of Hazara. Bahawalpur has a similar history of demand for a separate province, and that demand persists. A rally calling for the restoration of the province of Bahawalpur was held in August 2026.

New centres of gravity

Although each of these regions has its own history and political environment, what unites them is the desire for better access to the state’s institutions, greater representation and a greater share of development. Giving these areas their own “economic centre of gravity” would involve creating a new provincial capital with all its attendant institutions: universities would expand and hospitals would gain specialised departments, among other things, providing professional employment opportunities.

As the private sector responds to public investment and the movement of people, a region that relies heavily on a distant provincial capital for the income generated by administrative activity will, over time, begin to develop its own administrative and commercial ecosystems. This is when the issue of prosperity becomes most relevant.

Balanced development is also difficult to achieve where opportunity is spatially concentrated. Young people should not have to migrate to Lahore, Karachi or other large cities for opportunities such as quality education, decent jobs and access to specialist services. Establishing other centres of administration could help spread some of these opportunities.

There is also a simple administrative benefit. Governments can gain a more thorough overview of the people within smaller jurisdictions, attend to needs specific to the district and monitor the progress of schools, hospitals, roads and other such projects. Regional budgets can better reflect such differences in conditions.

Lessons from overseas

Regional experience offers similar examples. India created Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttarakhand in 2000 to give greater administrative and development focus to distinct regions, while Bangladesh later created Mymensingh as a separate administrative division.

Another example is Indonesia, which in 2022 created new provinces in Papua, stating that the goals were to shorten administrative reach, improve public services, make development more focused and reduce regional disparities. President Joko Widodo called the division an attempt to make development more equitable across a territory too large to be managed in this way. The comparison is relevant to Pakistan because of its own combination of population growth, geographical distance and differential development.

Local government is especially important. Prosperity spreads more effectively when authority reaches municipalities and districts rather than remaining concentrated at the provincial tier. Provincial restructuring can create the larger framework, while stronger local institutions carry that change into towns and communities.

The process also has to reflect public aspiration. Credible surveys, consultations and economic feasibility work can help establish where demand is strongest and what form people expect restructuring to take. The Constitution already provides a demanding route: Article 239 requires a constitutional amendment to receive two-thirds support in both Houses of Parliament, while an amendment altering a province’s limits also requires two-thirds approval of the affected provincial assembly. That framework gives administrative restructuring the scale of national reform it deserves.

Pakistan’s population will continue to grow. Its secondary cities will expand, regional economies will become more important and pressure on existing provincial centres will increase. Governance structures eventually have to respond to that reality. A more distributed administrative system offers a route towards a more distributed economy as well. More centres of government can mean more centres of education, healthcare, employment, investment and political representation.

For a country seeking broader prosperity, that is a possibility worth examining seriously.

item.title: Finding solutions to cost of living. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is unfortunate to see recent figures which showcase that tax relief has resulted in no real reduction in the unusually high or fluctuating market prices -- a clear disservice to consumers who deserve some financial relief on basic goods.
The government reduced duties and taxes on 63 essential commodities in the FY27 budget, including rice, pulses, edible oil, spices, and agricultural products. Yet prices of many of these goods have remained high or even increased.
Reducing taxes and duties on essential goods is a welcome step when the cost of living continues to put pressure on ordinary families. However, this glaring gap between policy and reality remains a serious concern.
There are legitimate factors behind some of these increases: Traders have pointed to higher fuel costs, energy shortages, floods, heavy rainfall, and disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
While these pressures cannot simply be dismissed, they should not become a blanket explanation for every price increase either.
The onus is, therefore, on the government to strengthen market monitoring and determine where the benefits of tax concessions are going. If importers, wholesalers, or intermediaries are absorbing the savings instead of passing them on, consumers are effectively being denied the relief that public policy intended to provide.
This is particularly important at this point in time, when household budgets are already stretched; recent reporting has found families cutting back on food and household necessities as everyday expenses continue to rise.
Tax reductions should be accompanied by transparency, competition, and effective oversight. Relevant agencies need to regularly compare import costs, wholesale prices, and retail prices, and take action where unjustified margins or manipulation are found.
The objective of tax relief should ultimately be clear: Making essential goods more affordable.
The government has taken the first step, but now it must ensure that the benefit actually reaches the people it was meant to help.

item.title: Saving Dhaka’s lakes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to strengthen coordinated efforts to prevent pollution and improve the environment of the lakes in Gulshan, Banani, Baridhara, Niketan, and Dhanmondi must be taken seriously and heeded.
For too long, these lakes, which ought to -- beyond being vital urban ecosystems that regulate drainage and reduce flooding -- provide respite and peace to the citizens of Dhaka, have instead been reduced to polluted messes as a result of years of sewage discharge, illegal connections, sludge buildup, and institutional neglect.
If Dhaka fails to act now with discipline and coordination, these fast-deteriorating water bodies will slip beyond recovery.
Of course, we are well aware that the pollution is not accidental. Sewage enters Gulshan Lake through at least a dozen identified points while buildings bypass proper sewerage systems and dump waste directly into stormwater drains. This is mismanagement and a lack of regard of the highest order, and needs immediate correction.
Beyond the coordination, and for Wasa and the city corporations to work together, we need people within the administration who recognize the magnitude of the issue and actually care to find solutions. There is simply no justification for the city’s lakes to be in such a polluted state, and that year after year, decade after decade, it has only gotten worse is embarrassing.
The deployment of special teams is encouraging, but teams alone cannot fix a system that has allowed pollution to flourish for decades. Dhaka needs accountability, with real consequences for offenders as well as those responsible for action but failing to do so.
As among the least liveable cities in the world, these water bodies must become clean, functional, and protected to offer some respite to an increasingly frustrated citizenry. With the PM himself recognizing the importance, there can be no more excuses.

item.title: A legacy written at the UN. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
At the United Nations General Assembly later this month, when Prime Minister Tarique Rahman speaks, he will enter a domain in which his parents have already spoken on behalf of what Bangladesh needed from the world.
This will add yet another page to a long political history that dates back almost half a century.
In 1980, President Ziaur Rahman addressed the United Nations at a special session which was dominated by the oil crisis and the growing economic gap between developed and developing countries. Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, meanwhile, first addressed the General Assembly in 1991, after the BNP’s election victory brought her to office as PM, and returned to the UN podium in 2005 during her third term.
Now Tarique Rahman is poised to make his speech during the 81st session of the General Assembly when Bangladesh will take the chairmanship.
It was different every time. The international system was different as well. There is, however, one thing in common: The need for Bangladesh to exercise its agency to define and pursue its national interest.
Ziaur Rahman expressed it in the language of 1980.
The oil shock had exposed how vulnerable poorer countries were to decisions made elsewhere. In his UN address, he questioned the imbalance between huge global military expenditure and declining development assistance. He linked international peace with the economic divide between rich and poor countries and called for changes to the global trade, financial, and development system.
For Bangladesh, he placed agriculture, rural development, and food production high on the national agenda. At the same time, he pressed developed countries for better market access, more development assistance, and debt relief.
His address was summed up in one phrase: “Self-reliance.” It was not a call for isolation. Ziaur Rahman was arguing for a Bangladesh that could rely more on its own productive capacity while working with other countries to secure a fairer international order.
Khaleda Zia’s first UN address came in a very different Bangladesh. The country had just returned to parliamentary democracy. The available material from her 1991 speech points to concerns that were immediate and national: Democratic governance, the sharing of common river waters, recovery from the April cyclone, rural development and poverty reduction, and greater attention to women’s education and maternal and child health.
The subjects were largely domestic. The forum was global. That was part of the point. Bangladesh was taking its own problems to an international audience, rather than allowing the country to be defined solely by the crises it faced.
By 2005, Khaleda Zia was speaking from a different position again. Her address covered UN reform, terrorism, human rights, development, the interests of least developed countries, and peacekeeping. Bangladesh was still making demands of the international system, but it was also presenting itself as a country with responsibilities within that system.
She pointed to Bangladesh’s contribution to UN peacekeeping and its role in international efforts on peace and security. The message was broader than development assistance: Bangladesh had interests to defend, but it also had something to contribute.
That thread helps put Tarique Rahman’s “Bangladesh First” policy in perspective. The phrase is new. The underlying instinct is older.
Ziaur Rahman spoke of self-reliance. Khaleda Zia placed democracy, development, sovereignty, and Bangladesh’s international responsibilities at the centre of her UN interventions. Tarique Rahman is now putting national interest more explicitly at the heart of his foreign-policy language.
There are parallels elsewhere. India’s Nehru-Gandhi family produced three generations of prime ministers. Sri Lanka’s Bandaranaike family saw political power pass across generations as well. But political inheritance does not come with a script. Every generation meets a different world.
That is where Tarique Rahman’s UN appearance becomes more than a family milestone. The world in which he will speak has almost nothing in common with the world in which Ziaur Rahman operated in 1980. Bangladesh is not the young nation overly dependent on foreign aid that it was then. Its economy, diplomatic interests, and international role have changed. So have the questions confronting it, from climate change and economic security to shifting geopolitical alliances and the Rohingya crisis.
The old question of national agency remains, but its meaning has become more complicated. A country cannot put its interests first simply by looking inward. The interests of Bangladesh are such that they are related to what goes on outside the country. Protecting national interests has become more about managing competing influences.
That is the test of any political legacy. Ziaur Rahman used the UN to argue for greater economic self-reliance and a stronger voice for developing countries. Khaleda Zia used it to speak about Bangladesh’s democratic transition, development concerns and responsibilities in international affairs. Tarique Rahman now has the opportunity to give his own meaning to “Bangladesh First.”
His speech will inevitably be compared with those of his parents. But the more useful comparison may be with the country itself. Bangladesh will be presiding over the General Assembly as Tarique Rahman speaks. The country that once went to the UN asking for greater room to develop is now in a position to shape part of the institution’s agenda.
That is perhaps the clearest measure of how much has changed since 1980. The family’s UN history, in that sense, is also a condensed history of Bangladesh’s changing place in the world. The central idea has survived, but the circumstances have not.
Jobair Babu is a filmmaker, columnist, and broadcaster.

item.title: Reimagining the ‘human’ in HR. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Artificial intelligence is no longer a distant vanguard discussed exclusively at Silicon Valley tech symposiums. It has fundamentally begun to reshape the topography of recruitment and workforce management in Bangladesh in concrete, measurable terms.
Consider a scenario numbers-driven HR professionals know all too well: A single entry-level vacancy in Dhaka can easily attract several thousand digital submissions. Where manual screening once demanded days of cognitive exhaustion and carried a profound risk of overlooking non-traditional yet highly qualified talent, AI-powered applicant tracking systems (ATS) and parsing algorithms can now sift through the deluge within minutes.
This transformation is unfolding across a diverse spectrum of the Bangladeshi economy stretching from multinational conglomerates and forward-thinking financial institutions to local enterprises and business process outsourcing (BPO) firms.
However, at present, employees harbour deep-seated anxieties regarding job security, middle management questions the long-term relevance of traditional supervisory roles, and organizations struggle to demarcate where human capability ends and machine intelligence begins.
This concern is far from unfounded. The pertinent question confronting us today is whether our institutional capacity for human adaptation can keep pace with technological acceleration equitably.
Human resources in Bangladesh must therefore transcend its legacy role of administrative processing and consciously assume a more visionary mandate: Becoming the deliberate architect of human potential in an AI-driven economy.
The most immediate demonstration of AI adoption in Bangladeshi HR is undisputed operational liberation. Automated resume screening, biometric, and AI-driven attendance metrics, algorithmic payroll configuration, and AI chatbots managing preliminary candidate communication have radically optimized workflows.
Yet, this efficiency does not exist in a vacuum; it arrives with a distinct societal cost.
A definitive study conducted by the Bangladesh Labour Foundation (BLF) in collaboration with researchers from BRAC University surveyed garment workers across the industrial hubs of Dhaka, Gazipur, and Narayanganj. The findings were sobering: Technological automation had already contracted overall employment in specific RMG segments by nearly one-third, with sweater production and woven-garment assembly lines bearing the brunt of the transition.
Crucially, those displaced were disproportionately helpers, older workers, and women with limited formal education -- the exact demographic possessing the fewest alternative economic prospects.
The socio-economic impact of this shift depends entirely on where a worker stands in the economy. The scope of automation varies drastically between sectors. In the manufacturing and RMG sectors, AI threatens to replace entire physical roles and eliminate low-skill positions, placing vulnerable labor at severe risk.
Conversely, in knowledge-intensive corporate environments, AI functions differently. It primarily automates discrete tasks rather than whole professions, augmenting human analytical power and reallocating valuable time toward strategic thinking
This is the stark reality that hyper-optimistic tech narratives often gloss over. In labour-intensive manufacturing, automation does not merely absorb tedious sub-tasks; it threatens to eliminate entire categories of entry-level employment.
Advanced computerized knitting machines and automated fabric cutters are shifting the industry standard. The ethical imperative for modern HR leadership is to mitigate this displacement deliberately through structured corporate retraining frameworks, upskilling initiatives, and equitable severance packages ensuring a "just transition" rather than a chaotic fallout.
Conversely, in knowledge-intensive corporate landscapes -- such as tech startups like Pathao and Chaldal, or pioneering mobile financial services (MFS) giants like bKash - the dynamic is entirely different. In these environments, AI acts as an augmentative tool rather than a replacement, automating repetitive tasks rather than whole professions.
When HR professionals in these settings are unburdened from the tyranny of bureaucratic paperwork, they gain the strategic bandwidth required to focus on macro workforce planning, employee mental well-being, and organizational culture. Bangladesh's AI narrative is not monolithic; it is a tale of two distinct workforces, contingent entirely upon a worker's position within the economic hierarchy.
The structural mismatch and the algorithmic bias
The most formidable structural bottleneck to our digital evolution remains the systemic mismatch between tertiary academic output and contemporary industry demands.
While progressive employers increasingly look for sophisticated digital literacy, data fluency, and adaptive analytical capabilities, conventional academic curricula often remain stuck in a legacy system that rewards memorization over applied reasoning. The modern corporate ecosystem no longer requires graduates to compete against machine intelligence; it requires professionals who can creatively collaborate with it.
Government initiatives have begun laying the groundwork to bridge this gap. The state has articulated ambitious targets to catalyze the ICT sector’s contribution to national GDP. However, the execution of most initiatives faces a critical challenge: The stark urban-rural digital divide. The infrastructure heavily favours metropolitan centres like Dhaka and Chittagong.
Furthermore, a less apparent but equally hazardous risk lies in the deployment of AI-driven recruitment engines. If an AI screening tool is trained on historical corporate data, it risks inadvertently encoding past biases -- such as disproportionately favouring resumes that feature elite, urban universities or specific affluent postal codes.
Without rigorous algorithmic auditing and conscious oversight by HR departments, these automated systems may institutionalize a digital glass ceiling, systematically excluding brilliant talent originating from rural or underprivileged backgrounds.
As machine learning systematically absorbs the administrative overhead of corporate operations, HR departments are uniquely positioned to reclaim their true purpose. The efficacy of a modern HR department should no longer be audited merely through the lens of cost reduction, but through the metrics of workforce resilience and sustained institutional learning.
This commitment to reskilling must cross the corporate threshold; it must extend directly to factory floors, where the vulnerability to displacement is highest and social safety nets are thinnest.
Ultimately, we must recognize the boundaries of this technology. While AI fundamentally excels at pattern scanning, data aggregation, and workflow automation, it cannot replace the human core.
AI is unrivaled at processing colossal data sets, identifying hidden operational patterns, and executing synchronous workflows. It cannot, however, emulate authentic human empathy, decipher subtle cultural nuances, navigate complex interpersonal conflicts, or provide ethical leadership during an organizational crisis.
Bangladeshi HR leaders must deliberately prioritize emotional intelligence, psychological safety, and ethical decision-making. We must build accessible internal pathways for current employees to acquire functional AI competencies, rather than short-sightedly replacing them with technology-native recruits.
Bangladesh finds itself at a unique historical crossroads. Our vast youth demographic represents an enviable macroeconomic asset that few ageing Western or East Asian nations possess. Yet, this demographic dividend is not a guarantee of prosperity; it is a time-sensitive window of opportunity.
To prevent widespread economic disenfranchisement, an integrated coalition of government institutions, academic policy-makers, corporate leaders, and HR strategists must collaborate. We must build a workforce capable of thriving in a hybridized economy, not merely within the air-conditioned corporate suites of Gulshan and Banani, but also across the industrial manufacturing zones of Gazipur, Savar, and Narayanganj.
AI will undoubtedly redefine the mechanics of labour, but its ultimate socio-economic outcomes must remain anchored by human purpose. The future will not belong to the organizations that achieve total, cold automation, but to those that leverage technology to make their workplaces more profoundly, equitably human.
Aninda Ghosh is senior assistant manager of human resources, University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB).

item.title: Bungling Asian Games chiefs play North Korean anthem for South. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Asian Games organisers played the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men’s hockey team on Friday, later apologising for the blunder.

South Korean officials were left angered by the latest mishap to hit the Games ahead of Saturday’s opening ceremony in Nagoya.

South Korea thrashed Bangladesh 5-0 but beforehand, instead of their national anthem, the song belonging to North Korea rang out.

The players from South Korea, who had lined up to listen to their anthem, looked at each other bemused.

Organisers then played Bangladesh’s anthem, before playing the South Korean anthem later, the South’s Yonhap news agency said.

However, the referee ordered players on both sides to shake hands with each other and to start getting ready to play before the anthem ended, it reported.

A stadium announcer apologised for the blunder but Min Tae-seok, coach of South Korea, was deeply unimpressed.

“This is a really serious problem. When we protested, they said, ‘We’re sorry. It wasn’t that it wasn’t prepared, there was a mistake on the part of those responsible for playing it’,” he said. “But this is something that simply should never happen.”

An official from South Korea’s Olympic committee said they were trying to find out what happened.

“We are currently looking into the matter to verify the exact facts,” the official told AFP.

The build-up to the Games has been overshadowed by complaints from teams about the quality and amount of accommodation.

Some teams were also stranded at the airport for up to six hours when they landed this week.

item.title: Japan cricketers hail 'amazing' experience playing India at Asian Games. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Japan’s women cricketers said they had an “amazing” experience at the Asian Games on Friday, despite the hosts being crushed by powerhouse India in the quarter-finals.

India, ranked behind only Australia and England, bowled out Japan for 57 off 19.5 overs in the Twenty20 contest.

Led by opener Shafali Verma’s unbeaten 40 off 15 balls, India romped to an eight-wicket victory by reaching 59-2 off just five overs.

Japan have appeared in two previous Asian Games and are benefiting from a push to promote cricket in the baseball-obsessed country, where it is a minority sport.

“This opportunity was amazing, especially for me,” said Japan’s Ahilya Chandel. “Being half-Indian, it was extra special. Watching the team on TV and now being able to face them in real life has been great.

“From this game we can learn a lot about what we can work on in the future, if we get to face them again or play higher-ranked teams.” A good-size crowd of home supporters turned out to watch Japan at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nagoya.

“Playing at home was really good and special,” said Chandel. “Friends and family came, along with supporters and our sponsors.

“There were probably fans who didn’t know cricket but came to watch because it was a new sport for them.

“That’s what we want as a women’s cricket team, to attract Japanese people who don’t know cricket.”

Defending Asian Games champions India will play Bangladesh in Sunday’s semi-finals and Pakistan face Sri Lanka.

Sri Lanka beat Malaysia by 86 runs in the day’s other quarter-final.

Tobacco price hike a step in the right direction. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government’s latest decision to raise cigarette prices, albeit only for low-tier cigarettes, is a step in the right direction, but it is nowhere near enough to confront the scale of Bangladesh’s tobacco crisis.
Bangladesh, regretfully, has one of the highest rates of tobacco consumption in the world, and reports more than 160,000 deaths every year from tobacco‑related illnesses.
As such, incremental price adjustments, while helpful, will not deliver the public‑health impact our country has urgently needed for some time now. Tobacco remains far too affordable, and affordability is among the largest drivers of consumption.
When prices rise, consumption drops -- especially among youth and low‑income groups, who are most vulnerable to tobacco addiction and most harmed by tobacco‑related disease.
Bangladesh’s current tax structure, however, continues to keep cigarettes within easy reach. Even after the latest increase, tobacco products remain cheaper here than in most comparable economies.
Tobacco continues to drain billions from the health system and fuels chronic diseases that burden hospitals year‑round. Every taka spent on treating tobacco‑related illness is a taka diverted from maternal health, child nutrition, and essential public services.
Despite making claims of wanting to be a tobacco-free nation in the next decade and a half, such a pledge remains hollow without serious interventions. As long as cigarettes are priced like everyday commodities, they will, naturally, be consumed like everyday commodities.
The government must move beyond modest adjustments and adopt a bold, health‑driven approach: Significantly higher taxes and strict enforcement to prevent under‑pricing and illicit sales.
Tobacco is killing Bangladesh, and affordability is enabling it. Prices must rise meaningfully if the country is serious about protecting public health and safeguarding its future.

item.title: Addressing river erosion requires more than temporary fixes. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest devastation along the Teesta -- with several hundred families losing homes, cropland, and stability overnight -- is yet another reminder that river erosion in Bangladesh is a permanent, structural threat.
Addressing erosion is and should have been recognized as a long‑term national priority. Yet, as locals who have lost everything overnight state, authorities often took measures only after houses began to collapse, rather than taking permanent steps to protect riverbank communities.
That thousands remain trapped in cycles of displacement, poverty, and uncertainty as a result of this reactive approach is infuriating, and demands attention.
Year after year, we should not be seeing families fleeing with whatever they can carry, homesteads collapsing into the river, and local administrations scrambling to provide temporary shelter.
Such stopgap measures may slow erosion for a moment, but they do nothing to protect communities in the long run. Bangladesh cannot continue relying on emergency responses that merely delay the inevitable.
Permanent solutions require a different mindset. Riverbank protection must be engineered, not improvised. Countries facing similar challenges have invested in multi‑year projects, reinforcing banks with sustainable materials, and restoring natural buffers. Bangladesh must adopt the same seriousness.
Erosion control also cannot be left to fragmented agencies working in isolation. Water resources authorities, local administrations, disaster‑management bodies, and environmental experts must operate under a unified national strategy, as without coordination, even well‑designed interventions will fail under bureaucratic confusion and overlapping responsibilities.
Bangladesh has the technical expertise and the institutional capacity to build lasting protection -- what it has lacked is urgency. River erosion is solvable, but only if we commit to long‑term planning and disciplined implementation. Above all, it requires the administration to recognize the suffering of these communities, and start caring beyond offering temporary fixes.

item.title: The case for revisiting VAT timing. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh wants a tax system that businesses trust, an investment climate that rewards the formal economy, and a treasury that can meet its bills without constant borrowing.
This July, the Finance Act 2026 moved us a long way towards the first two.
The Act, in force since July 1, cut VAT returns from 12 a year to four. It ended the rule that disallowed an expense whenever tax had not been deducted at source, lowered the deposit needed to contest a tax demand, and fixed income tax rates for five years.
Few budgets in recent memory have taken the cost of compliance this seriously. The finance minister and his team deserve full credit for it.
The third goal, however, is where the difficulty lies.
That is exactly why the National Board of Revenue's current look at quarterly VAT payment should be read with care, not alarm.
The reform bundled two separate things. One is how often a business files. The other is how often it pays.
Filing less often saves time and paperwork, and costs the state very little. Paying less often is different. It moves cash out of the treasury and into company accounts, and that has a price.
The numbers are not hard to work out. Under section 64 of the VAT Act , VAT used to be paid within 15 days of the end of each month. It is now paid within 15 days of the end of each quarter.
Assume sales are spread evenly through the month. Under the old system, the average VAT amount reached the treasury about a month after it was collected. Under the new one, VAT collected in the first month of a quarter waits about three months, in the second about two, and in the third about one. That is an average of two months. VAT now stays in private hands twice as long.
Estimates put the resulting float at roughly Tk20,000 crore. The government has to borrow to replace it, at a cost of about Tk2,000 crore a year, which implies an interest rate of around 10%.
Put simply, the state is giving registered businesses an interest-free loan and paying market rates to fund it.
In an ordinary year, the country could carry that cost. This year, it cannot do so comfortably.
The conflict in the Gulf has pushed Bangladesh back onto the spot market for LNG. The latest cargoes were approved at close to $30 per MMBtu, against the $10 to $12 we typically paid before the conflict.
Petrobangla estimates the conflict added Tk10,600 crore to the LNG subsidy in FY2025-26 alone. One study puts the extra fossil fuel import bill at up to $2.8 billion this year. None of these bills wait for the end of a quarter. They fall due cargo by cargo.
All of this lands on a revenue base that remains among the narrowest in the world relative to GDP.
This is a cash-flow problem, not a solvency one. But cash-flow gaps get filled with borrowed money, and the public pays the interest.
Then there is administration. The NBR has matched VAT records month by month for years. A quarterly cycle pushes back the point at which mismatches come to light, and research on tax compliance has long found that the chance of being caught shapes behaviour at least as much as the size of the penalty.
The NBR has been candid that its systems were not fully ready for the change, and it is now weighing a return to the old arrangement. Automatic eVAT enlistment and digital Mushak invoicing, both introduced by the Act, are the right long-term fix. They will need time.
Other countries have already worked through this problem.
India's QRMP scheme , introduced in 2021, lets goods and services taxpayers with turnover of up to Rs 5 crore file quarterly but pay monthly. Under its fixed-sum option, each of the first two monthly payments is 35% of the previous quarter's cash liability, so roughly 70% is paid before the return is filed.
The United Kingdom has run a payments on account regime since 1993. Businesses with annual VAT liabilities above £2.3 million make interim payments in the second and third months of each quarter, and settle the balance when they file.
In my view, the answer already sits within Bangladesh's own tax framework.
Our advance income tax asks taxpayers to pay in installments through the year and settle the balance later. I believe the same approach can be applied to VAT.
Keep the quarterly return exactly as it is. Ask businesses to pay around three-quarters of their estimated monthly liability each month, and settle the rest with the return.
On the same assumptions as before, the average holding period drops from two months to about one and a quarter. The treasury gets back roughly three-quarters of the float. Businesses keep the lighter paperwork and a quarter of the cash benefit. The change could start with larger taxpayers, where most of the float sits, and leave the smallest firms alone.
The finance minister has approached this question with the care it calls for. Rather than settle it by order, he has chosen to hear from business first, which is the surest way to protect confidence in a reform his own budget introduced.
A time-bound adjustment, with a clear point at which the full facility returns once energy import costs ease, would build naturally on that approach.
Businesses have a part to play as well. If they expect the state to keep its word, they should keep theirs, paying on time and keeping their invoicing records in order.
Taken as a whole, the government's handling of this issue is sound. It introduced the relief, recognized the pressure that followed, admitted where its systems fell short, and opened the question to consultation.
Asking that VAT, collected on the state's behalf, reach the treasury sooner does not add to anyone's tax bill. It is a reasonable request in an energy crisis, when the country is paying far more for imported LNG than it did before the conflict.
It simply matches the pace of public revenue to the pace of public spending. At a time like this, that is what sound fiscal management looks like.
Ashfaq Zaman is the chief strategist of the Dhaka Forum Initiative and a strategic international affairs expert.

item.title: The great gas robbery. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For the past two months, thousands of households in capital Dhaka have been held hostage by a deeply frustrating “double-billing” crisis -- forced to pay for gas they never get to burn.
Following a drastic drop in supply on July 21, reportedly attributed to a technical glitch at the Moheshkhali LNG terminal, millions of residents connected to Titas Gas lines have been unable to cook at home.
Yet, they are still forced to pay the fixed monthly bill of Tk1,080 simply to keep their connections from being disconnected.
This leaves consumers bearing a massive financial burden. They pay Titas for a service they are not receiving while simultaneously spending thousands more on market-rate LPG cylinders or facing higher electricity bills from using induction cookers.
Because postpaid residential gas billing in Bangladesh is based on a flat rate per burner, Titas charges for the mere existence of a connection, completely ignoring whether adequate gas pressure is actually available.
While Titas has been quick to issue standard public apologies for the “inconvenience,” the company has refused to consider the only rational remedy: Suspending billing for the months in which it fails to deliver gas.
It is a profound injustice that forces families to pay two or three times over, simply to cook their meals.
While mid-September brought some improvement in gas supply, the benefits largely went to industrial consumers rather than households still suffering from shortages.
As a resident of West Dhanmondi, my own kitchen has been without a gas flame since July 21. My family has had to rely entirely on rice cookers and multi-cookers.
Compounding the misery, routine electricity load-shedding has perfectly coincided with the gas shortages. Throughout my neighbourhood -- and in many others where friends and relatives live -- lunches and dinners are routinely delayed because the power goes out in the middle of cooking.
While induction cookers can generally be more cost-efficient than standalone LPG cylinders, constant load-shedding and successive electricity tariff hikes make them a stressful alternative.
In some affected areas of the city, pipelines briefly cough back to life during ungodly hours, forcing residents to choose between a good night’s sleep and cooking a meal between 2am and 4am.
In my neighbourhood, even that agonizing compromise is not an option; the supply has remained completely dead, day and night, since July 21.
As someone living in a rented apartment, I cannot even resort to “civil disobedience” by withholding payment. The landlord collects the fixed gas bill as part of the monthly rent. If landlords were to protest by refusing to pay Titas, the consequences would fall squarely on the tenants.
Ignoring the bills altogether invites aggressive disconnection drives. Titas field teams routinely disconnect physical lines over unpaid arrears, even in areas with zero gas pressure.
Resolving the resulting fines and navigating the reconnection process later is a massive bureaucratic headache that most ordinary citizens cannot afford to risk.
This leaves consumers wondering where to turn. Charging full bills for zero service raises serious questions about fundamental consumer rights and whether the Directorate of National Consumers’ Right Protection (DNCRP) could step in to spearhead a legitimate campaign on behalf of the public.
The Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB) has already openly criticised Titas, calling the practice of collecting monthly bills without supplying gas “tantamount to stealing from citizens.”
It has also noted that a simple acknowledgment of the problem is hollow without financial compensation or bill waivers.
Defenders of the utility might point to its fragile balance sheet. Now operating as a public limited company (PLC), with 25% of its shares traded on the Dhaka Stock Exchange, Titas is bleeding money.
In the 2024-25 fiscal year, the company suffered a net loss of Tk772 crore, marking its third consecutive year in the red, with cumulative losses reaching Tk1,680 crore.
Furthermore, Titas’ system losses climbed to a staggering 9.47%, far exceeding the 2% ceiling allowed by the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC).
But should ordinary households be forced to cushion a utility provider from its own financial failures?
If Titas is collecting flat-rate bills for gas it never delivers, why is it losing money?
The answer lies in deep-seated internal corruption and mismanagement. Titas loses billions of cubic feet of gas every year to “system losses” -- a euphemism for widespread gas theft through illegal pipelines allegedly supplying influential entities and unauthorized commercial hubs.
Because Titas cannot account for this stolen gas, revenue squeezed from law-abiding, non-metred households is effectively swallowed up in attempts to cover the cost of the missing fuel.
While Titas’s balance sheet is deeply troubled, that does not excuse the reality on the ground. Dhaka residents are effectively subsidizing systemic corruption and leakages with their hard-earned money, even as they pay out of pocket for alternative cooking methods simply to feed their families.
Somebody, somewhere, must be held answerable.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Bab al-Mandab chokepoint: What complete closure would mean for Pakistan. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bab al-Mandab may be far from Karachi, but the impact of its closure — if it happens — would be felt on our factory floors, in household budgets and in every vehicle that uses fuel. In Pakistan, the stakes are particularly high, as soaring shipping costs and delays to exports could put jobs at risk.

The Strait of Hormuz is already under stress and largely blocked to all ships, including tankers, while Houthi forces have escalated attacks on shipping and threatened a full naval blockade of Bab al-Mandab.

The Houthis seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait last week, declaring a maritime blockade on Riyadh. While the current blockade of Bab al-Mandab is limited to Saudi ships, fears of a larger closure persist.

As exporters, industrialists and regional experts weigh in on the possible implications of such a blockade for Pakistan, the question for Islamabad is no longer theoretical: what would happen to Pakistan’s economy if this 29-kilometre gateway between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean were to effectively close?

In the short term, the immediate impact of a closure of Bab al-Mandab would be felt by shipments using the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, particularly those involved in trade with Europe.

Shipping lines would have to divert affected services around the Cape of Good Hope, increasing voyage times and freight costs while putting additional pressure on vessel and container availability. The additional burden on trade and the economy would depend on the duration of the closure.

The stakes are considerably high — not only for Pakistan but for all trading nations — as roughly a tenth of all global seaborne trade, and about a third of Europe’s imports, moves through this corridor linking Asia, Europe and East Africa.

Now that this route is contested, ships sailing through it would not only put their crews at risk but would also have to pay hefty war-risk insurance premiums.

A safer option would be to divert around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope, a detour that typically adds 10 to 18 days to the journey, depending on several factors, including weather conditions. These longer voyages could cost well over a million dollars more in additional fuel and crew costs.

According to the Pakistan Ship’s Agents Association (PSAA), a cargo ship takes between 18 and 22 days to travel from Northern Europe to Karachi via the Bab al-Mandab and Suez Canal route. The journey from Karachi to the US East Coast, meanwhile, takes between 25 and 30 days. Taking the Cape of Good Hope route would add to these travel times, affect the reliability of delivery schedules and result in slower turnaround times.

With higher shipping costs and longer delivery times, Pakistani exporters — especially those in the textile industry — fear that their European customers may turn to alternative suppliers for their orders.

A prolonged closure of Bab al-Mandab would not only increase the cost of each shipment for Pakistani importers and exporters, but could also encourage European buyers to seek alternative trading partners.

Pakistan’s textile exporters are already under pressure as they compete with Bangladesh, Vietnam and India in European and American markets.

Longer lead times can strain just-in-time retail contracts, tie up working capital in goods in transit for longer and expose exporters to penalties for late deliveries. The compounding effect could widen the current account deficit, as costlier oil imports push up the import bill while more expensive and slower shipping erodes export receipts from the European Union and the US.

“We must act early to keep trade moving and protect our competitiveness,” Karachi Chamber of Commerce and Industry President Rehan Hanif said.

Fuel supply losses

The closure of Bab al-Mandab to Saudi ships has seriously affected fuel supplies. Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association Senior Vice Chairman Raja Wasim said crude oil for Pakistani refineries was previously supplied from Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports, but those supplies had since stopped.

He added that four to five vessels carrying refined oil products, including petrol and diesel, arrived each week from the Persian Gulf, but the number of such shipments had also declined.

As the war widened, the crucial Saudi East-West Pipeline in Saudi Arabia was hit as well. The pipeline carries crude oil from the oil-producing Dammam province, near Bahrain and Qatar on the Persian Gulf coast, across the Arabian Peninsula to Yanbu city on the Red Sea.

As a result, oil supplies to Pakistan have been disrupted. Describing the disruption to the route as worrisome, Wasim said that crude oil supplies from Yanbu to Pakistani refineries had completely stopped.

“We used to receive up to two tankers of crude oil on a weekly basis. The impact is visible; the petrol price has jumped by Rs30 per litre in the last 10 days,” Wasim said, adding that the current situation was not just about prices but also a lack of supplies.

“We are not like Japan or China, which can buy oil from American companies. Can we afford it?” he questioned.

Because Pakistan holds limited strategic fuel reserves and imports most of its refined petroleum products, almost every dollar of additional Gulf freight or insurance costs is eventually reflected in ex-depot prices.

Currently, Pakistan has several options available, but such scenarios also present an opportunity to look ahead, according to Islamabad Chamber of Commerce and Industry President Sardar Tahir.

He said Pakistan needed to diversify its energy sources, build strategic fuel reserves and smooth out price spikes linked to shipping disruptions, rather than passing them directly on to consumers.

“We need to focus on diversifying export markets as well as logistics, improving port efficiency and strengthening domestic production of critical inputs to help reduce our vulnerabilities,” Tahir said.

Meanwhile, analysts tracking the wider Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab crisis have warned that a coordinated disruption at both chokepoints could produce a self-reinforcing shock with regional repercussions.

Sanober Institute Executive Director Dr Qamar Cheema and strategic analysts studying the wider dual-chokepoint crisis said pressure on Pakistan to play a role in regional mediation efforts was growing, as sustained diplomatic engagement would be required to move towards de-escalation.

“Pakistan is now going to play a role in mediation. We can talk to the Houthis, just as the Americans did in Oman,” Cheema said, stressing that such talks were essential for the region and Pakistan.

item.description:
First there was a record deluge, then a shortage of beds, and now Asian Games organisers in Japan are “praying” that a typhoon does not play havoc with a cruise ship housing thousands of athletes.

More than 17,000 athletes and officials are descending on the port city of Nagoya and the prefecture of Aichi for the continent’s sporting showpiece.

To cut costs, there is no traditional athletes’ village. Instead, competitors are staying in temporary huts, hotels and the cruise ship Costa Serena.

Last week, record rainfall drenched Nagoya and forced participants briefly to evacuate the shipping container-style lodgings.

Several teams have complained about the quality of the huts, including the beds being too short, and others have said there are not enough rooms for everyone at the Games.

On Thursday, two days ahead of the opening ceremony, weather forecasters predicted that a typhoon could hit Japan’s main island – where Nagoya is situated – on Sunday or Monday.

That would have repercussions for the estimated 4,000 Games participants housed on the cruise ship floating in Nagoya’s port.

“All we can do is to pray that the worst-case scenario will not happen,” The Asahi Shimbun quoted an unnamed sports federation official as saying.

The newspaper noted that the course of the storm Dujuan “remains uncertain”, but said one of the more severe consequences would see the ship evacuated from the port area and relocated.

September and October is typhoon season in Japan.

Thursday was dry and sunny in Nagoya, but wet weather in previous days meant the women’s cricket match between China and Bangladesh was abandoned without a ball being bowled.

About 104mm (four inches) of rain fell in an hour in Nagoya on Tuesday last week, prompting municipal officials to issue an evacuation order for parts of the city.

Rainwater seeped into several competition venues.

Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of weather events in Japan and elsewhere.

item.title: Pakistan women survive Thailand scare to make Asian Games semi-finals. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan survived a serious scare to win the quarter-final of the Asian Games Women’s Cricket Competition against Thailand by three wickets at the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin, Japan on Thursday.

Put in to bat by Pakistan, Thailand posted 91 runs in the designated 11 overs following rain delay before Pakistan went deep and left only two balls to spare as they crossed the finish line.

Fatima Sana’s side had also lost seven wickets in the process and it was the captain’s 21 off 13 after opener Shawal Zulfiqar’s 25 off 14 that kept Pakistan in the game, despite the usually talismanic Fatima losing her wicket before finishing the job.

Thailand had got off to a brisk start, scoring 41 runs in the powerplay on the back of a productive 24 off 22 balls from Nannapat Koncharoenkai. Fatima had drawn first blood with the ball, dismissing Natthakan Chantham for six runs.

Koncharoenkai took the attack to Tuba Hassan and Umm-e-Hani, hitting the latter for 14 runs off the eighth over, as she stitched a solid 65-run stand with Phannita Maya.

A dropped catch by wicket-keeper Gul Feroza and lapses in the field aided Thailand as they raced to 72 off 9 overs, when Maya was retired out on a 16-ball-15.

Nauremol Chaiwai smoked Nashra Sandhu for a six and a four before falling to her on the next ball, getting caught by Fatima.

It was the skipper only who finally dismissed Koncharoenkai in the last over of the shortened innings, the batter narrowly missing out on a half-century as she was trapped lbw for a 38-ball-49; Fatima ended with figures of two for 22 in her three-over spell.

Shawal starts strong

Shawal, and fellow opener Gul Feroza, gave Pakistan a strong start to the chase, scoring two boundaries in the first over. She followed it up with a six off Maya’s bowling in the second.

Both Gul and Shawaal were dropped in the third and fourth overs respectively, but the openers kept the scoreboard ticking before Shawal was caught and bowled by Onnicha Kamchomphu, who took a well-judged catch.

The first wicket triggered a collapse which saw Thailand take four wickets in 13 balls.

Ayesha Zafar came out to bat at one-drop, and was dismissed almost immediately, falling in the next over to Suleeporn Laomi, with Thailand pulling back some control as Pakistan finished the fifth over at 39-2.

Kamchomphu picked up her second wicket as Gul was stumped by keeper Koncharoenkai, with Pakistan finding themselves in a serious wobble at 43-3, which turned into 47-4 as the experienced Aliya Riaz went boundary-and-out in the same over.

Thailand conceded just one run in the seventh over, tightening their grip on the match as Pakistan ominously sunk further.

Fatima, batting at number four, then reeled back momentum by hitting Kamchomphu for three fours and a six in the ninth over, joined by a six off the batting of Eyman Fatima.

The captain fell on the first ball of the following over, and was followed by Eyman in the next as Pakistan again found themselves in some bother at 76-7.

A six and a four off Sunida Chaturongrattana’s bowling by Tuba Hassan took the equation to less than run-a-ball for Pakistan, and following her dismissal to the same bowler, Umm-e-Hani and Eman Naseer took Pakistan over the line in the last over.

Earlier, China’s cricket return to the Asian Games for the first time in 12 real came to a halt before a ball was even bowled. Their quarter-final fixture against Bangladesh in Nagoya was first delayed due to a wet outfield, and eventually called off without a toss.

Bangladesh proceed to the semi-finals, owing to their higher seeding.

Both semi-finals will be held on Sept 20 at Nisshin. Pakistan will take on the winners of tomorrow’s quarter-final clash between Malaysia and Sri Lanka, while Bangladesh will meet the winners of the later fixture between India and Japan.

item.title: All in on nuclear. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is encouraging to see Bangladesh’s reaffirmation of its commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear science -- one that is both timely and pivotal for its future.
Science and Technology Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam stressed the importance of safety, security, international cooperation, and using nuclear technology for public welfare while representing Bangladesh at the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) 70th General Conference in Vienna recently.
It is no secret that nuclear technology can offer significant benefits to a developing country like Bangladesh. Its applications extend well beyond electricity generation, with the IAEA’s technical cooperation having supported Bangladesh in areas including healthcare, agriculture, food, water management, industry, and energy for more than five decades.
The newly signed Country Program Framework for 2026-2032 could further expand these opportunities, while the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant is also expected to contribute to Bangladesh’s energy security and efforts to reduce carbon emissions.
However, such benefits can only be meaningful if nuclear development is accompanied by the highest standards of safety and accountability. The country’s commitment to international conventions on spent fuel and radioactive waste management is therefore significant, and must be reflected in practice.
Equally important will be ensuring that the benefits of nuclear science reach ordinary people. The minister’s emphasis on cooperation through the IAEA’s Rays of Hope initiative, particularly to expand access to cancer treatment, is a welcome reminder that technological advancement should ultimately improve lives.
As Bangladesh expands its nuclear capabilities, transparency, professional oversight, and preparedness must remain central. There can be no room for complacency when dealing with technology that requires such high levels of expertise and responsibility.
Peaceful nuclear development should serve national needs while contributing to sustainable development and public welfare. Bangladesh should, therefore, continue strengthening its institutions, expertise, and international partnerships so that the promise of nuclear technology is realized safely, responsibly, and for generations to come.

item.title: Public safety cannot be overlooked. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Two recent incidents in Dhaka have once again raised serious concerns about public safety and security: A crude bomb blast at Dhaka University, and a 24-year-old man being hacked to death while getting a haircut at a salon on the same day.
These incidents, while different in nature, point to the same underlying, urgent concern: Ordinary people must be able to go about their daily lives without fearing sudden violence. A university campus, a roadside salon, a marketplace, or a residential neighbourhood should not become places where people are exposed to explosives, weapons, or violent attacks.
The Dhaka University blast is particularly troubling because such incidents can quickly create panic among thousands of students and others who use the campus every day.
To that end, the authorities must determine who was responsible, how the explosives were brought onto the campus, and whether there were warning signs that could have been detected earlier. Security measures should be strengthened without turning educational institutions into unnecessarily restrictive spaces.
At the same time, the killing in Keraniganj shows that public safety is not limited to high-profile locations. When people can be attacked in ordinary places in broad daylight, it raises uncomfortable questions about policing, criminal networks, weapons, and the ability of law enforcement to deter violence.
The government has a fundamental responsibility to protect citizens, but effective security also requires accountability after crimes occur. Investigations must be prompt, impartial, and thorough, while those responsible must face due process and punishment where guilt is established.
People cannot be expected to feel secure simply because authorities pledge greater vigilance. The safety being promised must be visible in practice -- through stronger policing, effective intelligence, rapid responses, and consistent enforcement of the law.
Bangladesh needs to ensure that its people feel -- and indeed are -- safe, and that can only be achieved if violence is not allowed to become an accepted part of everyday life.

item.title: Before we celebrate inclusive jobs, we must build inclusive schools. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is aiming to build a more inclusive workforce. The government is hiring persons with disabilities. Companies are introducing diversity policies. Corporate leaders increasingly view inclusion as both a social responsibility and a business necessity.
These are all positives, and ought to be celebrated.
However, what we need is not simply recruitment policies or employment quotas, but something much more basic. While inclusive jobs should be celebrated, inclusive education needs greater focus.
The end of inclusion is employment, and the journey starts with education.
Bangladesh does not know exactly how many persons with disabilities it has; however, according to the Department of Social Services, about 3.84 million persons with disabilities are registered in the country.
The country's educational infrastructure presents a different picture. There are only about 56 government-funded special schools for children with disabilities in Bangladesh, a remarkably low number for a nation of 180 million people.
The shortage is clearer when compared with the need. The Department of Primary Education reports that only about 81,000 children with disabilities are enrolled in primary education, and government scholarships cover a similar number. This means only a small proportion of the millions of persons with disabilities are included.
The issue is not simply the number of schools; it is also where those schools are located.
Specialized institutions are mainly in Dhaka and other large cities. In most rural districts, specialized education is out of reach for families. Parents must either move at high financial cost or give up the idea. Many children stay home because no suitable school is nearby. For many families, the path to employment stops before it starts.
When employers advertise inclusive jobs, the outcome is predictable. Human resources departments struggle to find qualified applicants with disabilities, not for lack of talent but because opportunities were denied years earlier.
This shows a contradiction in the way we have adopted a national policy.
We celebrate inclusive recruitment because it is visible. Appointment ceremonies make headlines, and companies receive recognition for diversity and inclusion.
Yet classrooms that produce tomorrow’s workforce receive less attention. We invest more energy in the pipeline’s end than at its beginning.
If children with disabilities cannot access a good education, they are less likely to complete secondary school, pursue higher education, receive technical training, or acquire the skills employers seek.
Although Bangladesh aims to become a knowledge-based, upper-middle-income economy, millions remain excluded from the system that develops human capital.
That is not just a question of social welfare; it is an economic issue.
Bangladesh often discusses productivity, the demographic dividend, and the need for a skilled workforce. Yet each child excluded from education is a talent the country will never develop.
Excluding people with disabilities from education now shrinks the future workforce, reduces productivity, and slows economic growth.
Inclusion therefore is an investment in national competitiveness.
Globally, emphasis has shifted towards inclusive education, in which ordinary schools serve all learners through accessible facilities, trained teachers, assistive technologies, accessible materials, and specialized support. Special schools will always play an important role for children needing intensive support, but they should not be the only option.
Bangladesh has a long way to go. Many schools lack basic facilities for students with disabilities, and there must be a greater focus on inclusive physical infrastructure. Yet, inclusive education also requires preparing teachers, adapting curricula, providing classroom support, and ensuring children receive appropriate help from an early age.
By promoting diversity and inclusion, corporate Bangladesh can strengthen the talent pipeline before recruitment begins. Through CSR and ESG initiatives, companies can fund inclusive classrooms, offer scholarships, provide assistive technologies, train teachers, offer internships, give students with disabilities career advice, and help develop their skills.
Many jobs place excessive emphasis on formal academic qualifications and overlook practical skills, potential, and reasonable workplace adjustments. An inclusive labour market should recognize ability alongside credentials.
The appointment letters issued deserve praise because they show progress and offer hope. But we should not take appointments to mean there is systemic inclusion.
The true test of our success will not be the number of appointment ceremonies we hold, but whether a child with a disability in Kurigram has the same opportunity as a child in Dhaka to learn, develop skills, and compete for a job.
Inclusive employment does not begin when the appointment letter is handed over; it starts years earlier, when a child first enters a classroom and believes they belong.
Bangladesh has demonstrated a desire to create inclusive workplaces. The next challenge, however, is much bigger: Establishing an education system that gives every child, regardless of disability or place of birth, an equal chance of reaching those workplaces.
Until such a system is in place, inclusive employment will continue to be an admirable achievement for a small number of people rather than a real opportunity for most.
Shafiq R Bhuiyan is working at BRAC Bank as a Vice President and Head of Internal Communication and CSR.

item.title: Do global university rankings reflect Bangladesh’s higher education and labour market needs?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every year, global university rankings generate considerable excitement in Bangladesh. BUET, DU, NSU -- who ranked where? We spend days discussing whether a university has moved up or down, entered a particular global list, or fallen further behind internationally recognized institutions. Then, of course, come the social-media fights.
There is nothing wrong with paying attention to global rankings. But we rarely ask a more fundamental question: What exactly are these rankings designed to measure, and are those measures aligned with what Bangladesh currently needs from its universities?
The global university ranking industry is relatively young. The Shanghai Ranking was first published in 2003, initially as an effort to assess how Chinese universities compared with leading research universities worldwide.
QS and Times Higher Education (THE) jointly launched a global ranking in 2004 before separating in 2009. These rankings emerged as higher education was becoming increasingly global.
Their methodologies reflect that environment. In THE's World University Rankings, 59% of the overall score comes directly from research environment and research quality.
Even its “teaching” category includes measures such as the ratio of doctoral to undergraduate students and doctorates awarded per academic staff member.
QS uses a different methodology and places more weight on employability, but half of its current score falls under what it calls “research and discovery,” based on academic reputation and citations per faculty.
There is nothing unreasonable about these measures. They make sense for universities competing globally for research funding, scholars, doctoral students, and scientific prestige. Rankings are also useful to internationally mobile students choosing among universities and countries they may know relatively little about.
Bangladesh, however, is not competing in this market on the same scale.
Our universities primarily educate Bangladeshi students; large numbers of international students are not coming to Bangladesh for higher education.
Internationalization can certainly be an aspiration. But if the immediate task for most of our universities is to provide high-quality education to Bangladeshi students and prepare them for our labour market, should global research visibility be such an important benchmark of their success?
Bangladesh needs high-quality research. We need institutions capable of producing serious scholarship, training PhD students, and contributing to scientific and technological development.
But that does not mean every university should try to imitate a large research-intensive Western university.
There is also a labour-market question. How many research-trained graduates does Bangladesh currently need, and where will they work?
Expanding research-oriented graduate education without a corresponding expansion in research institutions, R&D-intensive industries, and other employers capable of using those skills will not, by itself, create a research economy.
The United States, for example, has major research universities but also liberal arts colleges, regional universities, community colleges, and institutions primarily focused on undergraduate teaching.
They are not all expected to perform the same function. Bangladesh should similarly ask what it most urgently needs from higher education.
I would argue that improving the quality of the four-year undergraduate degree should be one of our highest priorities.
And there is plenty to improve.
Students should have greater freedom to choose and change majors. Credits should be transferable across departments and eventually across universities.
Engineering students should be able to study economics, writing, history, or philosophy; economics students should be able to acquire meaningful training in mathematics, computing, or environmental science.
A university education should combine specialization with broader intellectual development.
We also need to examine faculty recruitment. The practice of hiring very recent graduates as lecturers, sometimes directly from the same departments in which they studied, and putting them immediately onto long-term academic career tracks deserves scrutiny.
Universities need transparent hiring, meaningful evaluation, professional development, and clearer distinctions between teaching and research expectations.
University quality is also about institutional culture. Sexual harassment, bullying, intimidation, and abuse of authority are not peripheral issues.
An institution that performs well on publication metrics while failing to provide students with a safe and professional environment cannot reasonably be called an excellent university.
Nor should we ignore what happens after graduation. Experiential learning, internships, hands-on training, writing and communication skills, quantitative and digital skills, and exposure to workplaces should matter.
If most graduates will enter professional employment rather than academic research, how well a university prepares them for that transition should be part of how we evaluate it.
Interestingly, Bangladesh already has an informal ranking system. An 18-year-old applying to university knows that particular institutions and departments are more competitive than others.
Families and employers make similar distinctions. What we lack is a transparent and systematic way of measuring quality.
Perhaps we should build one.
A Bangladesh-specific framework could evaluate institutions according to their missions. Undergraduate-focused universities could be assessed on teaching quality, faculty qualifications, curriculum, facilities, student support, experiential learning, graduate outcomes, and institutional environment, with research as one component rather than the dominant one.
Program-level rankings could be even more useful. A university may have an excellent economics program but a weak science department, or a strong business school but inadequate laboratory sciences.
A single number for an entire university hides information that students actually need.
None of this means Bangladesh should ignore international rankings. Universities aspiring to compete internationally as research institutions should absolutely pay attention to them.
But global rankings should not determine our entire understanding of what makes a good university.
Aparna Howlader is an Assistant Professor of Economics at Chatham University, Pittsburgh, USA.
